For 4.3: pnpm build is the gate that stops a broken publish; a private or unshaped package under packages/ fails it by name.
FINAL (agent session 2026-11-14). LANDED as one commit, 26f6e30 on origin/main of crab-shack/capabilities ("Every package has a publishable shape: built daemon half, layer and migrations as source"), parent 642513e. Same tree as the paused head a148cbd; the three WIP commits were squashed. Nothing is published. Platform pin still 0.7.1. Worktree and branch 94z-4-1 removed. This note stands alone; the PAUSED note above is superseded except where it gives more detail.

WHAT EACH KIND OF PACKAGE PUBLISHES (all sixteen: version 0.1.0, not private, a one-sentence description, repository.directory, publishConfig registry https://npm.pkg.github.com, access restricted).
- Capability or connection (the 14 cap-* and plugin-* packages): one entry, the root ".". In the workspace "exports" is ./src/index.ts; publishConfig.exports replaces it at pack time with { types: ./dist/index.d.ts, default: ./dist/index.js }. The root entry exports the definition factory (acpDefinition, botsDefinition, chatClaudeCodeDefinition, chatCodexDefinition, deploymentsDefinition, issuesDefinition, teamDefinition, uptimeDefinition, claudeCodeDefinition, codexDefinition, herokuDefinition, netlifyDefinition, repositoryDefinition, slackDefinition). "files" is dist, plus for a package with a web layer nuxt.config.ts, app/ and (where the layer imports it) src/wire.ts as source, plus src/migrations where there is one (cap-bots, cap-deployments, cap-issues, cap-team, cap-uptime, plugin-repository). The webLayer field still names the layer id (13 packages; cap-acp has none).
- @crab-shack/claude-acp: "." is dist/index.mjs with dist/index.d.mts, "./package.json", and the bin claude-acp at dist/cli.mjs. It keeps .mjs because cap-acp launches dist/cli.mjs by path (found with require.resolve('@crab-shack/claude-acp/package.json')).
- @crab-shack/capabilities-testing: "." is dist/index.js; its build copies fake-acp-agent.mjs and claude-fixture.mjs beside the modules. It runs the shim through tsx from source in the workspace and from the installed dist/cli.mjs otherwise. The fake Slack Socket Mode server now lives here (startFakeSocketMode, nextEnvelopeId), no longer in plugin-slack's entry.
- Rule for what a layer imports from src: only src/wire.ts, shipped as source beside the layer; dist holds its compiled copy for the daemon half. Anything else a layer came to import by relative path must be added to "files" (the check says so).
- Migrations are found at run time by package name: src/package-root.ts takes dirname(dirname(require.resolve('<own name>'))), which is the package root both for src/index.ts and for dist/index.js, so the root entry must stay exactly one directory deep.

HOW IT IS BUILT. Each package has "build": "tsdown" and a tsdown.config.ts (entry src/index.ts, unbundle, platform node, fixedExtension false so .js/.d.ts, dts, deps.neverBundle: one output file per source module, nothing bundled). tsdown is a root devDependency only. Root "build" is "turbo run build && node scripts/check-packages.mjs". Lint, typecheck, test and pnpm dev need nothing built (shown again today with every dist removed). The lockfile's packages and snapshots sections are byte-identical to the ones before this commit; only importers changed.

PEER OR DEPENDENCY. Peers: @crab-shack/platform-daemon and @crab-shack/platform-sdk as "0.x" on the 14 capabilities (platform-sdk only on capabilities-testing), with the exact 0.7.1 in devDependencies; every capability named in a definition's dependsOn as workspace:^ (published as ^0.1.0), with workspace:* in devDependencies; vue as an optional peer on the 13 layer packages. nuxt and @nuxt/ui are deliberately NOT peers (see pnpm findings). Dependencies: drizzle-orm, hono, zod, marked, ws, @agentclientprotocol/sdk, @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp, and @crab-shack/claude-acp (workspace:^, on cap-acp, cap-bots and capabilities-testing).

HOW A PRODUCT INSTALLS AND LISTS A CAPABILITY. (1) Add the package and every capability it peers on to "dependencies" of BOTH apps, the daemon app and the web app (cap-acp too, though it has no layer; otherwise pnpm auto-installs it for the web app separately). (2) Daemon app: import the factory from the package's root entry and add it to the definition list. (3) product.yaml: the id under capabilities, the plugin type id under pluginTypes for a connection, the layer id under layers when the package has webLayer, and the capability under a module if it has views or agents. (4) The web app finds the layer through the webLayer field of the dependency's package.json; nothing else to wire. (5) A product generated by platform-new product has tests that state its composition (apps/daemon/src/product.test.ts, apps/web/test/unit/distribution.test.ts) and they must be edited. Leaving out something a capability needs stops the daemon at boot: "Capability 'chat-claude-code' depends on 'acp', which is not in the definition list."

WHAT scripts/check-packages.mjs ENFORCES (per package under packages/, on the tarball pnpm pack writes). Fails the build, naming the package, when it: is private; has no description; does not publish to npm.pkg.github.com with restricted access; still names a workspace:, link: or file: range in dependencies, peerDependencies or optionalDependencies after packing; (a capability) has any entry besides "."; names an export or bin target the tarball lacks or that is not under dist; ships a test file (test/, test-support, *.test.*); leaves out or changes any file of src/migrations; has webLayer but no nuxt.config.ts or leaves out a file of app/; ships layer files without webLayer; has a layer file importing a relative path the tarball lacks; imports a package it does not list in dependencies or peerDependencies (type-only imports of nuxt and @nuxt/ui from layer files are the one exception). "node scripts/check-packages.mjs --out <dir>" keeps the sixteen tarballs. A package the generator writes (platform-new capability) is private and unshaped, so pnpm build fails naming it until it gets a sibling's manifest fields and tsdown.config.ts.

PROVED TODAY (logs in scratch .../fdc913cc-.../scratchpad/94z-4-1/final and proof/, alone/, e5/).
- Fixture product from platform-new product with cap-chat-claude-code, cap-acp, plugin-claude-code, plugin-repository from tarballs: gates pass; built daemon under plain Node applies platform (2), board (1), repository (1), second boot 0; web pages render; one copy of each. NEW: the Claude Code connection was logged in through its own start-login and submit-code actions against a fake claude, a chat turn ran through the installed cap-acp launching the installed claude-acp dist/cli.mjs, and a headless Chromium rendered chat-claude-code's ModelEffort component in the prompt bar (Default model / Opus / Sonnet / Haiku; screenshots in final/prompt-bar). Drivers: scripts/proof.sh, scripts/check-prompt-bar.sh, scripts/browser.mjs.
- Alone: install 404 naming @crab-shack/cap-acp today; boot refusal naming acp when pnpm resolves the peers; ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND naming @crab-shack/cap-acp with autoInstallPeers false.
- All sixteen installed (the development distribution copied to scratch, workspace:* replaced by tarball URLs, scripts/e5.sh): lint, typecheck, test (daemon 82, web 5), build pass; built daemon under plain Node applies the 7 migration sets and registers 16 capabilities, second boot 0; built web app serves the shell, setup pages and each feature capability's page; one .pnpm directory and one lockfile snapshot per package and one each of platform-*, nuxt, @nuxt/ui, vue, drizzle-orm, hono, zod. No defect found.
- Migrations byte-identical to 7590af1: 18 files in 6 packages, tree hashes equal. The command in the PAUSED note (pathspec 'packages/*/src/migrations') matches no file and proves nothing; use ':(glob)packages/*/src/migrations/**'.

PNPM FINDINGS (pnpm 12.15).
- A capability that peers on nuxt or @nuxt/ui (optional or not) is installed TWICE in a product whose daemon app has a build tool whose rolldown differs from the one nuxt's peer range picks: pnpm resolves Nuxt's peer graph per app. With vue as the only web peer there is one copy. Do not add nuxt or @nuxt/ui as peers.
- blockExoticSubdeps is on by default: a product installing tarballs or git URLs needs blockExoticSubdeps: false and an override for every @crab-shack package another one depends on or peers on. Not needed once they come from the registry.
- autoInstallPeers is on by default: once published, a missing peer is fetched silently, so the guarantee is the daemon's boot check, not the install. With autoInstallPeers false the install only warns ("pnpm peers check" lists them) and the boot fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND.
- A project that pins an older platform keeps it: a peer "0.x" resolves to the product's pinned version, not the newest. "0.x" accepts 0.8.0 and would not refuse a platform too old for a capability.
- A product lists capabilities in both apps' dependencies; listing only layer packages in the web app makes pnpm install the rest for the web app on its own.

FOR 94z.4.2 (Changesets). Sixteen independent versions, all 0.1.0. Sibling peers are workspace:^ (published ^0.1.0): at 0.x a minor bump of a capability takes its dependents out of range, so Changesets must bump dependents (peer dependents included) when a capability gets a minor. cap-acp, cap-bots and capabilities-testing depend on claude-acp as workspace:^. The apps (@crab-shack/daemon, @crab-shack/web) are private and must be ignored. The check script refuses a workspace: range that survives packing, so publish through pnpm (pnpm publish or changeset publish run by pnpm), which rewrites them.
FOR 94z.4.3 (first publish). pnpm build is the gate: it must run before any publish, since dist is not in git and "files" would otherwise ship an empty package (the check fails on a missing built entry). publishConfig already carries registry and access. CI has never run the Build step with the check on a runner (Test fails first; see below). Publish order does not matter for install, but a product cannot install any of the 14 until all the peers it names exist in the registry.
FOR 94z.5.1 (Candy Mountain consuming these). Install each package in both apps; import only root entries (test support is not published: Candy Mountain's app tests today import only root entries, checked); plugin-slack no longer exports startFakeSocketMode, it comes from @crab-shack/capabilities-testing (a devDependency). If the daemon is bundled with the capabilities inside (tsdown alwaysBundle), migrations are still found by package name, but cap-acp then resolves @crab-shack/claude-acp and @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp from the daemon app, so the app must list both (not exercised); left external (the default) the built daemon imports each capability's dist from node_modules and nothing more is needed. The web typecheck of a generated product excludes root node_modules, so an installed layer is typechecked only where something included refers to it.
FOR 94z.6.1 (the command that adds a capability). It has to do steps (1) to (5) above: both apps' dependencies including the peers (read peerDependencies of the package, minus platform-* and vue), the factory import and entry in the daemon's definitions (factory name is the camel-cased id plus "Definition", exported from the root entry), product.yaml (capabilities, pluginTypes for plugin-*, layers when webLayer is set, a module entry), and the product's composition tests. scripts/list-caps.py and scripts/add-caps.mjs in the scratch directory do exactly this for the fixture and can be read as a specification.
FOR 94z.3.7 (platform pin). Peers are "0.x" and need no change; only the exact 0.7.1 pins in devDependencies, the apps and pnpm-workspace.yaml's minimumReleaseAgeExclude move.
FOR 94z.3.8 (CI). On this commit CI passed Install, Lint, Typecheck and failed Test in claude-acp (two standalone-executable tests at 5000ms), Build skipped. The same weakness reproduces on this machine when all 17 test tasks run at once under load: "TURBO_FORCE=true pnpm test" failed 4 of 4 here on this commit's tree and 2 of 2 on 642513e, always in claude-acp (the standalone-executable tests, and permissions.test.ts "cancelling the turn releases a pending decision", which sleeps 20ms and then asserts), once also cap-issues watcher.test.ts (a 2000ms waitFor). claude-acp alone passes 66 of 66. CI also shows plugin-claude-code "fails an attempt whose CLI never shows a link" (promptTimeoutMs 200) failing on the runner, on this run and on the run for 0dcf164 before it.

All five acceptance criteria shown by the agent on the landed tree (fixture product from tarballs incl. the prompt bar; alone fails naming cap-acp; one copy; nothing built for gates or dev). title: Capabilities: README and agent instructions for the repository
description:
Context: three repositories on this machine, all Jack's (GitHub user kingrea, the only developer).

The base (github.com/crab-shack/platform, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/platform) is a pnpm 12 workspace run through Turborepo that holds the platform. It publishes five packages to GitHub Packages (npm.pkg.github.com, scope @crab-shack, private) at one shared version (0.5.0 at the time of writing): platform-daemon (the Hono daemon over SQLite via Drizzle, with a /testing entry that is the daemon test kit), platform-web (the web shell, a Nuxt layer published as source, with the layer-list helper that finds a capability's layer from the webLayer field of a dependency's package.json), platform-sdk (wire types, the product configuration type, defineCapabilityDefinition and the capability contract), platform-config (the tsconfig, ESLint and vitest presets every package extends, the cm-packages boundary lint and its package-boundaries helpers, the commands platform-link, platform-unlink and platform-check-linked, and the generators platform-new capability, connection and product) and platform-cli. Beside them, unpublished: packages/cap-template and packages/plugin-sample (the worked examples the generators copy), and apps/ with a root product.yaml (the base's own development distribution). docs/ holds capability-authors.md, linking.md, registry-access.md, upgrade-path.md, capability-majors.md and product-file.md; CONTRIBUTING.md holds the changeset rule.

Candy Mountain (github.com/kingrea/candy-mountain-v3, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/candy-mountain-v3, where this bead tracker lives) is a product built on the base. Today it also holds the source of sixteen shared packages under its own scope @candy-mountain: eight feature or service capabilities (packages/cap-acp, cap-bots, cap-chat-claude-code, cap-chat-codex, cap-deployments, cap-issues, cap-team, cap-uptime), six connections that each bring the one plugin type their id names (packages/plugin-claude-code, plugin-codex, plugin-heroku, plugin-netlify, plugin-repository, plugin-slack), the Claude Code ACP shim (packages/claude-acp) and shared test support (packages/testing). The product itself is packages/candy-mountain (plain data) and thin apps: apps/daemon lists every capability definition and runs the platform's runDaemon, apps/web extends platform-web and the capability layers, apps/cli is the bin.

The capabilities repository (github.com/crab-shack/capabilities, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/capabilities) is where those sixteen packages are moving. Each is published on its own, at its own version, as @crab-shack/cap-<id>, @crab-shack/plugin-<id>, @crab-shack/claude-acp and @crab-shack/capabilities-testing. A product then picks capabilities by depending on them, as it already depends on the platform, and can write its own beside them. Capability ids, plugin type ids, layer ids, table names and migration histories never change in this move, because an existing database identifies each capability's migrations by its id.

A capability is one package with a daemon half (a definition made with defineCapabilityDefinition, exported from the package's root entry as a factory, stating its own package name and the SDK major it targets) and, when it has UI, a web half (a Nuxt layer at the package root). It owns its tables and its own migration history. A product is plain data (name, theme, scope label, and the id lists of capabilities, modules, plugin types and layers) joined at boot with the capability definitions; the daemon refuses to boot, naming the offender, when they disagree.

Commits: in the base and in the capabilities repository Jack has authorised agents to commit and push to main when a piece of work is finished, and once a repository's fast lane exists that push is also the release; follow the agent instructions file in that repository where there is one. In Candy Mountain do not commit or push unless the orchestrator tells you to. The plan this bead comes from is in Candy Mountain at .ai-docs/plans/shared-capabilities/, for background only: this bead is complete without it.

The capabilities repository has packages and a development distribution but nothing telling a person or an agent what it is or how to work in it.

Write the root README as the map of the repository:
- What the repository is: the shared capabilities and connections for products built on the @crab-shack platform, each published as its own package at its own version.
- A table of the packages: name, whether it is a feature capability, a service-only capability, a connection, or support, one sentence on what it does, and which other packages it needs. Take this from each package's manifest and definition, not from memory.
- The platform version the repository pins and where that is set.
- Installing (the private registry and the token, by pointing at the base's docs/registry-access.md, not repeating it), the commands for the four gates, and how to run the development distribution.
- How to start a new shared capability or connection here with the platform's generator (pnpm platform-new capability, or connection), and that the result must be added to the development distribution.
- How to try an unreleased platform change here (pnpm platform-link, pointing at the base's docs/linking.md).
Leave a clearly marked Releasing section with one line saying it is written when the release flow lands; another bead fills it.

Write the agent instructions file at the root:
- Work in this repository is tracked in Candy Mountain's bead tracker (/home/kingrea/work/candy-mountain-v3, the bd command); this repository has no tracker of its own.
- Jack's standing permission: agents commit and push to main here when a piece of work is finished.
- Capability ids, plugin type ids, layer ids, table names and existing migration files are never changed; a schema change is a new migration.
- Point to the README for commands.

Plain prose, short. Do not describe anything that does not exist yet.
acceptance_criteria:
- The README has each section listed, and its package table matches the packages and their declared needs.
- The agent instructions file states the four points listed.
- Every command the README gives runs as written from a fresh clone.

Its agent added a short Run section to the README; the package table has no rows for product.yaml and the apps. Candy Mountain's apps/daemon/README.md (639 lines on how each capability's daemon half behaves) was not brought over and has no home here: do not copy it in this bead, but say in your report whether the README should point somewhere for it. 94z.4.1 (publishable shape) is still in progress: describe only what is on main.

Releasing section is a stub for the release-flow bead. apps/daemon/README.md of Candy Mountain (639 lines on daemon-half behaviour) not brought over; README does not point at it. Generator quirk: platform-new connection refuses an id containing 'sample'.

The base (github.com/crab-shack/platform, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/platform) is a pnpm 12 workspace run through Turborepo that holds the platform. Candy Mountain (github.com/kingrea/candy-mountain-v3, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/candy-mountain-v3, where this bead tracker lives) is a product built on the base. Today it also holds the source of sixteen shared packages under its own scope @candy-mountain: eight feature or service capabilities (packages/cap-acp, cap-bots, cap-chat-claude-code, cap-chat-codex, cap-deployments, cap-issues, cap-team, cap-uptime), six connections that each bring the one plugin type their id names (packages/plugin-claude-code, plugin-codex, plugin-heroku, plugin-netlify, plugin-repository, plugin-slack), the Claude Code ACP shim (packages/claude-acp) and shared test support (packages/testing). The product itself is packages/candy-mountain (plain data) and thin apps: apps/daemon lists every capability definition and runs the platform's runDaemon, apps/web extends platform-web and the capability layers, apps/cli is the bin.

The capabilities repository (github.com/crab-shack/capabilities, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/capabilities) is where those sixteen packages are moving. Each is published on its own, at its own version, as @crab-shack/cap-<id>, @crab-shack/plugin-<id>, @crab-shack/claude-acp and @crab-shack/capabilities-testing. A product then picks capabilities by depending on them, as it already depends on the platform, and can write its own beside them. Capability ids, plugin type ids, layer ids, table names and migration histories never change in this move, because an existing database identifies each capability's migrations by its id.

A capability is one package with a daemon half (a definition made with defineCapabilityDefinition, exported from the package's root entry as a factory, stating its own package name and the SDK major it targets) and, when it has UI, a web half (a Nuxt layer at the package root). It owns its tables and its own migration history. A product is plain data (name, theme, scope label, and the id lists of capabilities, modules, plugin types and layers) joined at boot with the capability definitions; the daemon refuses to boot, naming the offender, when they disagree.

The plan this bead comes from is in Candy Mountain at .ai-docs/plans/shared-capabilities/, for background only: this bead is complete without it.

The capabilities repository holds the capability packages but nothing that runs them. Until now Candy Mountain's apps were where capabilities were started, clicked through and tested together, and Candy Mountain is about to stop holding capability source. Capability work needs its own place to run.

Give the repository a development distribution, as the base has for its template: a daemon app and a web app over a product description that enables every capability, connection, plugin type and layer in the repository, so pnpm dev starts something in which every feature can be used. The apps a product generated by platform-new product has are the shape to start from. The product is described by a product.yaml and must not be called Candy Mountain; its modules can follow Candy Mountain's grouping.

Candy Mountain's apps also hold the tests that exercise capabilities together and the checks that the daemon's definitions, the apps' dependencies and the product lists agree (in apps/daemon and apps/web, including the capability-packages test and the distribution tests). Those that are about capabilities, rather than about Candy Mountain as a product, belong here now: bring them over and make them pass against this distribution. Leave Candy Mountain's copies alone; a later bead removes them.

The distribution is never published.

title: Jack: create crab-shack/capabilities and clone it beside the platform checkout
description:
Context: three repositories on this machine, all Jack's (GitHub user kingrea, the only developer).

The base (github.com/crab-shack/platform, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/platform) is a pnpm 12 workspace run through Turborepo that holds the platform. Beside them, unpublished: packages/cap-template and packages/plugin-sample (the worked examples the generators copy), and apps/ with a root product.yaml (the base's own development distribution). docs/ holds capability-authors.md, linking.md, registry-access.md, upgrade-path.md, capability-majors.md and product-file.md; CONTRIBUTING.md holds the changeset rule.

Candy Mountain (github.com/kingrea/candy-mountain-v3, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/candy-mountain-v3, where this bead tracker lives) is a product built on the base. Today it also holds the source of sixteen shared packages under its own scope @candy-mountain: eight feature or service capabilities (packages/cap-acp, cap-bots, cap-chat-claude-code, cap-chat-codex, cap-deployments, cap-issues, cap-team, cap-uptime), six connections that each bring the one plugin type their id names (packages/plugin-claude-code, plugin-codex, plugin-heroku, plugin-netlify, plugin-repository, plugin-slack), the Claude Code ACP shim (packages/claude-acp) and shared test support (packages/testing). The product itself is packages/candy-mountain (plain data) and thin apps: apps/daemon lists every capability definition and runs the platform's runDaemon, apps/web extends platform-web and the capability layers, apps/cli is the bin.

The capabilities repository (github.com/crab-shack/capabilities, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/capabilities) is where those sixteen packages are moving. Each is published on its own, at its own version, as @crab-shack/cap-<id>, @crab-shack/plugin-<id>, @crab-shack/claude-acp and @crab-shack/capabilities-testing. A product then picks capabilities by depending on them, as it already depends on the platform, and can write its own beside them. Capability ids, plugin type ids, layer ids, table names and migration histories never change in this move, because an existing database identifies each capability's migrations by its id.

A capability is one package with a daemon half (a definition made with defineCapabilityDefinition, exported from the package's root entry as a factory, stating its own package name and the SDK major it targets) and, when it has UI, a web half (a Nuxt layer at the package root). It owns its tables and its own migration history. A product is plain data (name, theme, scope label, and the id lists of capabilities, modules, plugin types and layers) joined at boot with the capability definitions; the daemon refuses to boot, naming the offender, when they disagree.

Commits: in the base and in the capabilities repository Jack has authorised agents to commit and push to main when a piece of work is finished, and once a repository's fast lane exists that push is also the release; follow the agent instructions file in that repository where there is one. In Candy Mountain do not commit or push unless the orchestrator tells you to. The plan this bead comes from is in Candy Mountain at .ai-docs/plans/shared-capabilities/, for background only: this bead is complete without it.

The shared capabilities are moving to their own repository, and no agent can create a repository in the crab-shack organisation or decide its settings.

Create a private repository named capabilities in the crab-shack GitHub organisation (github.com/crab-shack/capabilities), empty, with main as its default branch. Clone it to /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/capabilities, beside the platform checkout, and add it to the crab-shack VS Code workspace. Make sure GitHub Actions in that repository may publish packages to the organisation (the same organisation settings the platform repository relies on) and may read the @crab-shack/platform-* packages.

platform-link, in platform-config, points a product at a local checkout of the base so a platform change can be tried in the product before it is released; platform-unlink puts the registry versions back, and platform-check-linked (run by lint and by a pre-commit hook) stops a linked state being committed. docs/linking.md describes all three. The link knows only the five platform packages.

Capabilities are moving to their own repository and products will install them from the registry. Capability work then needs the same loop: change a capability in the local checkout and see it in a product at once, with no release in between. This is what keeps publishing out of moment-to-moment work, which matters because Jack wants nothing in the way while the capabilities are in active development.

Extend linking so a product can link to a local capabilities checkout, on its own or together with a base checkout, and unlink cleanly from either or both. A capabilities checkout is an installed pnpm workspace whose packages/ folder holds @crab-shack packages (cap-<id>, plugin-<id>, claude-acp and capabilities-testing) that export TypeScript source in the checkout and pin one platform version. Only the packages the product already depends on are linked; linking never adds a capability to a product.

The guarantees are the ones the platform link gives today, and they must hold in every combination:
- One copy of every library the product shares with what it is linked to. With both checkouts linked there are three installs in play, and the product, the platform and the capabilities must still load one copy of each shared library between them.
- Nothing but the product's workspace file, lock and node_modules is touched; no package.json and neither checkout.
- Unlinking restores the product byte for byte when nothing else changed while linked, and otherwise keeps the developer's edits as it does now.
- The guard catches a capabilities link left in place.
- Like the platform link, it refuses to run in CI, and a product's built output is not expected to run while linked.

The path can always be given explicitly and through the environment. The capabilities repository may not exist when you do this, so test against a fixture of the same shape. title: Base: the package checks cover installed capability packages
description:
Context: three repositories on this machine, all Jack's (GitHub user kingrea, the only developer).

The base (github.com/crab-shack/platform, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/platform) is a pnpm 12 workspace run through Turborepo that holds the platform. It publishes five packages to GitHub Packages (npm.pkg.github.com, scope @crab-shack, private) at one shared version (0.5.0 at the time of writing): platform-daemon (the Hono daemon over SQLite via Drizzle, with a /testing entry that is the daemon test kit), platform-web (the web shell, a Nuxt layer published as source, with the layer-list helper that finds a capability's layer from the webLayer field of a dependency's package.json), platform-sdk (wire types, the product configuration type, defineCapabilityDefinition and the capability contract), platform-config (the tsconfig, ESLint and vitest presets every package extends, the cm-packages boundary lint and its package-boundaries helpers, the commands platform-link, platform-unlink and platform-check-linked, and the generators platform-new capability, connection and product) and platform-cli. Beside them, unpublished: packages/cap-template and packages/plugin-sample (the worked examples the generators copy), and apps/ with a root product.yaml (the base's own development distribution). docs/ holds capability-authors.md, linking.md, registry-access.md, upgrade-path.md, capability-majors.md and product-file.md; CONTRIBUTING.md holds the changeset rule.

Candy Mountain (github.com/kingrea/candy-mountain-v3, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/candy-mountain-v3, where this bead tracker lives) is a product built on the base. Today it also holds the source of sixteen shared packages under its own scope @candy-mountain: eight feature or service capabilities (packages/cap-acp, cap-bots, cap-chat-claude-code, cap-chat-codex, cap-deployments, cap-issues, cap-team, cap-uptime), six connections that each bring the one plugin type their id names (packages/plugin-claude-code, plugin-codex, plugin-heroku, plugin-netlify, plugin-repository, plugin-slack), the Claude Code ACP shim (packages/claude-acp) and shared test support (packages/testing). The product itself is packages/candy-mountain (plain data) and thin apps: apps/daemon lists every capability definition and runs the platform's runDaemon, apps/web extends platform-web and the capability layers, apps/cli is the bin.

The capabilities repository (github.com/crab-shack/capabilities, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/capabilities) is where those sixteen packages are moving. Each is published on its own, at its own version, as @crab-shack/cap-<id>, @crab-shack/plugin-<id>, @crab-shack/claude-acp and @crab-shack/capabilities-testing. A product then picks capabilities by depending on them, as it already depends on the platform, and can write its own beside them. Capability ids, plugin type ids, layer ids, table names and migration histories never change in this move, because an existing database identifies each capability's migrations by its id.

A capability is one package with a daemon half (a definition made with defineCapabilityDefinition, exported from the package's root entry as a factory, stating its own package name and the SDK major it targets) and, when it has UI, a web half (a Nuxt layer at the package root). It owns its tables and its own migration history. A product is plain data (name, theme, scope label, and the id lists of capabilities, modules, plugin types and layers) joined at boot with the capability definitions; the daemon refuses to boot, naming the offender, when they disagree.

Commits: in the base and in the capabilities repository Jack has authorised agents to commit and push to main when a piece of work is finished, and once a repository's fast lane exists that push is also the release; follow the agent instructions file in that repository where there is one. In Candy Mountain do not commit or push unless the orchestrator tells you to. The plan this bead comes from is in Candy Mountain at .ai-docs/plans/shared-capabilities/, for background only: this bead is complete without it.

Products are about to take capabilities as dependencies from the registry instead of holding them in their own workspace. The checks a product runs over its capability packages cannot see them: the package-boundaries helpers in platform-config find capability packages by walking the product's workspace, and the distribution test that uses them (the capability-packages test in the base's apps/daemon, which platform-new product copies into every generated product and which Candy Mountain has its own copy of) only looks at what that walk returns. So for an installed capability nothing confirms that it is both a dependency of the daemon app and listed in the daemon's definitions, that the capabilities its definition depends on are the ones its package.json declares, that it follows the rule that only a plugin- package brings a plugin type, or that its stated SDK major agrees between package.json and definition. Some of these checks also assume every capability carries the product's own scope.

Make every check a product runs over its capability packages cover the capability packages its daemon app depends on from node_modules as well as the ones in its workspace, under any scope, reporting problems in the same words. A product that mixes its own capabilities with installed ones gets one answer covering both. The base's own distribution test uses the result, so a product generated by platform-new product is covered without anyone editing it.

Things to hold to:
- A published capability declares the other capabilities it needs as peer dependencies, so that a product ends up with exactly one copy of each. The dependency check must accept a peer dependency as declaring that need, for workspace and installed packages alike.
- An installed capability's daemon half is built output, not TypeScript source. The checks must work from what a published package actually contains.
- The rule that a capability lives in a folder named after it applies only to workspace packages.
- A product whose capabilities are all in its workspace gets exactly the results it gets today.

The base has no installed capability to test against. Give the tests one in whatever way is cheapest to keep honest, for example a packed copy of the sample connection.

The change carries a changeset and is released by pushing to main (the base's fast lane).
acceptance_criteria:
- In a product generated by platform-new product, with one capability installed from a tarball rather than the workspace: leaving it out of the daemon's definitions makes the product's tests fail, naming the package and what is missing; listing it makes them pass.
- An installed capability whose definition depends on a capability its package.json does not declare is named by the check; declaring it as a peer dependency satisfies the check.
- An installed capability whose package.json and definition disagree about the SDK major, or that breaks the plugin-type rule, is named.
- The base's four gates are green and its distribution test exercises at least one installed capability.
- A workspace-only product (run the base's own distribution and, linked, Candy Mountain) reports the same results as before.
- The release containing this is in the registry.
notes: Released in platform 0.6.0 (commit 31d1f9d on crab-shack/platform main; Release run 43371435289, CI run 43371435309 green). New export from @crab-shack/platform-config/package-boundaries: capabilityPackageProblems(packages, { daemon, listed, definitions }) returns { placement, registration, dependencies, sdk, kind } (string[] each), the distribution's capability-package checks over workspace and installed capabilities with the old messages; the folder rule applies only when !pkg.installed. capabilityDependencyDrift now accepts peerDependencies as a declaration (message says 'in its peerDependencies' when the declaration is a peer). apps/daemon/src/capability-packages.test.ts in the base (and so platform-new product output) calls it. Candy Mountain's own copy of that test still has inline checks with a '@candy-mountain/' folder rule that would misfire on an installed @crab-shack capability: 94z.5.1 should replace its checks with one capabilityPackageProblems call (listed: Object.keys(DEFINITIONS), definitions: capabilityDefinitions(), daemon: packages.get('@candy-mountain/daemon')). An installed cap-/plugin- package is indexed only if its peerDependencies name @crab-shack/platform-sdk (from 0.5.4).
close_reason: Released as platform 0.6.0 (commit 31d1f9d, minor: new export capabilityPackageProblems). The distribution test and capabilityDependencyDrift cover installed capability packages under any scope and accept peer dependencies.

title: Base: release from main without waiting (the fast lane)
description:
Context: three repositories on this machine, all Jack's (GitHub user kingrea, the only developer).

The base (github.com/crab-shack/platform, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/platform) is a pnpm 12 workspace run through Turborepo that holds the platform. It publishes five packages to GitHub Packages (npm.pkg.github.com, scope @crab-shack, private) at one shared version (0.5.0 at the time of writing): platform-daemon (the Hono daemon over SQLite via Drizzle, with a /testing entry that is the daemon test kit), platform-web (the web shell, a Nuxt layer published as source, with the layer-list helper that finds a capability's layer from the webLayer field of a dependency's package.json), platform-sdk (wire types, the product configuration type, defineCapabilityDefinition and the capability contract), platform-config (the tsconfig, ESLint and vitest presets every package extends, the cm-packages boundary lint and its package-boundaries helpers, the commands platform-link, platform-unlink and platform-check-linked, and the generators platform-new capability, connection and product) and platform-cli. Beside them, unpublished: packages/cap-template and packages/plugin-sample (the worked examples the generators copy), and apps/ with a root product.yaml (the base's own development distribution). docs/ holds capability-authors.md, linking.md, registry-access.md, upgrade-path.md, capability-majors.md and product-file.md; CONTRIBUTING.md holds the changeset rule.

Candy Mountain (github.com/kingrea/candy-mountain-v3, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/candy-mountain-v3, where this bead tracker lives) is a product built on the base. Today it also holds the source of sixteen shared packages under its own scope @candy-mountain: eight feature or service capabilities (packages/cap-acp, cap-bots, cap-chat-claude-code, cap-chat-codex, cap-deployments, cap-issues, cap-team, cap-uptime), six connections that each bring the one plugin type their id names (packages/plugin-claude-code, plugin-codex, plugin-heroku, plugin-netlify, plugin-repository, plugin-slack), the Claude Code ACP shim (packages/claude-acp) and shared test support (packages/testing). The product itself is packages/candy-mountain (plain data) and thin apps: apps/daemon lists every capability definition and runs the platform's runDaemon, apps/web extends platform-web and the capability layers, apps/cli is the bin.

The capabilities repository (github.com/crab-shack/capabilities, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/capabilities) is where those sixteen packages are moving. Each is published on its own, at its own version, as @crab-shack/cap-<id>, @crab-shack/plugin-<id>, @crab-shack/claude-acp and @crab-shack/capabilities-testing. A product then picks capabilities by depending on them, as it already depends on the platform, and can write its own beside them. Capability ids, plugin type ids, layer ids, table names and migration histories never change in this move, because an existing database identifies each capability's migrations by its id.

A capability is one package with a daemon half (a definition made with defineCapabilityDefinition, exported from the package's root entry as a factory, stating its own package name and the SDK major it targets) and, when it has UI, a web half (a Nuxt layer at the package root). It owns its tables and its own migration history. A product is plain data (name, theme, scope label, and the id lists of capabilities, modules, plugin types and layers) joined at boot with the capability definitions; the daemon refuses to boot, naming the offender, when they disagree.

Commits: in the base and in the capabilities repository Jack has authorised agents to commit and push to main when a piece of work is finished, and once a repository's fast lane exists that push is also the release; follow the agent instructions file in that repository where there is one. In Candy Mountain do not commit or push unless the orchestrator tells you to. The plan this bead comes from is in Candy Mountain at .ai-docs/plans/shared-capabilities/, for background only: this bead is complete without it.

Releasing the platform today takes three waits. The release workflow runs on every push to main and runs lint, typecheck, test and build before anything else. It then hands over to the Changesets action, which opens a "Version Packages" pull request that a person has to merge. Merging it runs every gate again and only then publishes. Jack is the only developer and the platform is in active development, so each wait is pure delay; it is the main thing slowing him down, and an agent cannot finish the loop at all because it cannot merge a pull request. Several pieces of upcoming work each need a platform release.

Give the base a fast lane, on by default, with one switch that turns today's careful flow back on.

While the fast lane is on:
- A push to main is the release. There is no pull request to open and no generated release pull request to merge. A change to a platform package states its version bump in the same push, and those versions are published without any further human step.
- Publishing does not wait for the checks. Lint, typecheck and tests still run on every push and report red or green, but beside the publish rather than before it. The only thing that stops a publish is a package that does not build.
- Nobody has to pull an automated commit before pushing again. If the release wrote versions or changelogs back to main, the developer's next push would collide with it and the delay would return in another form, so the pushed commit must already hold the versions.
- An agent can release. The repository has no agent instructions file today; add one saying that agents have Jack's standing permission to commit and push to main when a piece of work is finished, that under the fast lane this push is the release, and what a change to a platform package must carry.
- Publishing from a laptop is the documented fallback for when the workflow itself is broken: say what it needs and how.

What must not change: the five platform packages keep one shared version (the Changesets fixed group) and the SDK's exported version stays in step with it; every change to a platform package still carries a changeset and lands in each package's changelog; the per-package tags and the one tag for the shared version are still pushed; the packages are published to GitHub Packages with restricted access using the workflow's own token, as now; the workflow that checks pull requests keeps working for anyone who opens one.

The switch: one documented setting restores today's behaviour (the checks gate the publish, and changes arrive by pull request) without rewriting the workflows. The README's Releasing section and CONTRIBUTING.md describe today's flow only, and say that the release workflow runs the versioning step and that nobody publishes from a laptop; rewrite both so they are true for both positions of the switch and say which one the repository is in. Note there that enforcing pull requests on a private repository needs a paid GitHub plan the organisation does not have, so until then that half of the gate is a convention.

A second repository (the capabilities repository) will copy this lane, so keep it self-contained and easy to copy.

Non-goals: the CI workflow that platform-new product writes into a generated product is not changed. Nothing about what the packages contain changes.
acceptance_criteria:
- With the switch in its default (fast) position, pushing a commit to main that changes a platform package and states a patch bump results in all five packages at the new version in the registry, with no pull request opened or merged by anyone, and with the per-package tags and the shared version tag pushed.
- After that release, a second push from the same clone made without pulling succeeds.
- A push whose tests fail still publishes, and the checks for that push are visible as failed.
- With the switch in the gated position, a push whose tests fail publishes nothing.
- A push with no pending version change publishes nothing and fails nothing.
- The repository has an agent instructions file stating the commit and push permission and the changeset rule; README and CONTRIBUTING.md describe both positions of the switch, where it is, and the laptop fallback.
- This work itself was released through the fast lane as a patch.
notes:
Fast lane done in crab-shack/platform (commits 3a7f42e..5aa2329). Platform is now at 0.5.3 (0.5.1 = this work via the fast lane; 0.5.2 = fast-lane publish with a deliberately red test; 0.5.3 = gated-lane demo, published once green). All five packages and tags @crab-shack/<pkg>@0.5.x + v0.5.x exist for 0.5.1-0.5.3.
Switch: GitHub repository variable RELEASE_LANE on crab-shack/platform. Unset or "fast" = fast lane (default, current). "gated" = old flow (gates first, Changesets "Version Packages" PR). Flip: gh variable set RELEASE_LANE --body gated --repo crab-shack/platform ; back: gh variable delete RELEASE_LANE --repo crab-shack/platform. Any other value fails the release run.
Under the fast lane a change to a platform package carries a changeset APPLIED before the push: write .changeset/x.md, run pnpm version-packages (bumps all five, SDK_VERSION, changelogs, deletes the changeset), commit all of it, push to main = release. A leftover unapplied changeset on main fails the release run and publishes nothing. Checks (ci.yml) run beside the publish and do not gate it; only a build failure (or SDK_VERSION mismatch) stops it. AGENTS.md (+ CLAUDE.md -> @AGENTS.md) in the base states this.
Copying to capabilities: copy .github/workflows/release.yml (fast + gated jobs), scripts/unreleased.mjs (generic: changesets ignore list + pnpm ls + <name>@<version> tags on origin; --tag mode tags missing ones), root scripts version-packages and release (= build && changeset publish), ci.yml concurrency (per-sha on push). Drop the platform-only SDK_VERSION check and v<version> tag. Gotcha: changeset publish makes annotated tags and silently skips them without a git identity, so the fast job sets git user before publishing. No secrets needed (GITHUB_TOKEN with contents+packages write).
close_reason: Fast lane live in crab-shack/platform (repository variable RELEASE_LANE: unset/fast or gated). Released as 0.5.1; demonstrations 0.5.2 (fast, red tests) and 0.5.3 (gated). AGENTS.md, README and CONTRIBUTING.md cover both lanes. Evidence in bead notes.

title: Phase 5: one command adds a capability, and a catalogue lists them
description:
Adding a published capability to a product becomes one command instead of four edits in four files, and someone starting a product can see what capabilities exist before choosing.

Human test (Jack): generate a product with platform-new product. List the available capabilities from inside it. Add the Claude Code chat capability with one command and confirm it brought the ACP runtime and the Claude Code and repository connections with it and said so. Run the gates green, start the product, put the capability in a module, and open its page. Run the same command again and confirm it refuses because the capability is already there.

title: Phase 4: Candy Mountain runs on the published capabilities
description:
Candy Mountain depends on the published capabilities at exact versions and deletes its own copies. This is the proof that the move worked: an existing database keeps working and the product is thin.

Human test (Jack): on a machine with a database from before this phase, confirm the repository has no cap-* or plugin-* folder, then start Candy Mountain. The daemon's boot log shows no migration applied. Every existing plugin instance is healthy, a chat thread starts on each family, a bot runs, uptime and deployments read as before. Link to the capabilities checkout, change a label there and see it in Candy Mountain, then unlink and confirm git status is clean. Publish that change, move Candy Mountain to the new version of that one capability, and see the label in a build.

title: Phase 2: the capabilities repository exists and runs on its own
description:
The sixteen shared packages move to github.com/crab-shack/capabilities with their history, renamed to the @crab-shack scope, in a repository that is itself a small product: a development distribution with every capability enabled, where capabilities are run and tested without Candy Mountain. Candy Mountain is not touched in this phase.

Human test (Jack): from a fresh clone, install, run the four gates green and start the development distribution. Create a workspace, enable every module and confirm the features work as they do in Candy Mountain: an issue is created, a chat thread starts on Claude Code and on Codex, a bot runs, an uptime check reports, the deployments page reads a live version. Search the packages for "Candy Mountain" and "@candy-mountain" and find nothing outside history and changelogs.

title: Phase 3: capabilities are published, with the fast lane
description:
Each package in the capabilities repository is published under its own version, in a shape a product can install and run, and the repository gets the same fast release lane as the platform: a push to main publishes, checks run beside the publish, and one switch restores the gate.

Human test (Jack): change a label in one capability, state the version bump and push to main. Without opening anything on GitHub, see the new version on the organisation's packages page within a few minutes, and see that no other package's version moved. Break a test on purpose and push: the checks run red and the publish still happens. Flip the switch, push the same kind of change with a red test, and confirm nothing is published. Flip it back. In a scratch product generated by platform-new product, install two capabilities where one needs the other, build the product and start its built daemon and web app.

title: Phase 1: the platform treats an installed capability like a local one
description:
Today the platform's checks and its link command only know capabilities that sit in the product's workspace. Once capabilities arrive from the registry, the same checks must cover them and a product must be able to link to a local capabilities checkout to see a change without a release.

Human test (Jack): in a product generated by platform-new product, install one capability from a packed tarball rather than the workspace. Leave it out of the daemon's definitions and confirm the product's tests name it. Add it and confirm they pass and the app shows it. Then link the product to the checkout the tarball came from, change a label there, see it in the running product, unlink, and confirm git status is clean.

title: Phase 0b: the platform releases from main without waiting
description:
The platform repository gets a fast release lane: a push to main publishes, with no pull request, no generated release pull request and no waiting on checks, and one documented switch restores the gate later. Jack asked for this because the current loop (wait for the gates, merge, merge the release pull request) is his main blocker while the platform is in active development, and later phases each need platform releases.

Human test (Jack): change a line of a platform package's README, state a patch bump and push to main. Without opening anything on GitHub, see all five packages at the new version on the organisation's packages page within a few minutes. Push again from the same clone without pulling. Break a test on purpose and push: the checks run red and the publish still happens. Flip the switch, push a change with a red test, and confirm nothing is published. Flip it back.
close_reason: Only child 94z.1.1 closed; platform at 0.5.3 through the fast lane.

title: Shared capabilities: capabilities leave Candy Mountain for crab-shack/capabilities and are published one package each
description:
Candy Mountain's capabilities and connections move to their own repository, github.com/crab-shack/capabilities, where each is published as its own package. A product picks the ones it wants by depending on them and writes its own beside them. At the end Candy Mountain holds no capability source, a second product uses some of the same capabilities at versions it chooses, and a fix made once reaches every product that takes the new version.

Why now: a second platform is about to start and needs several of these capabilities. Copying the packages would fork each capability's tables and migration history, and every fix would have to be ported by hand.

Plan: .ai-docs/plans/shared-capabilities/overview.md and one document per phase. Phase 0a (Candy Mountain on platform 0.5) is the existing beads candy-mountain-v3-8by.4.12 to 8by.4.14 and is not repeated under this epic. Sub-epics are not chained to each other: ordering is carried by the task beads, so work that can run at the same time does.

Human test (Jack): on a machine with an existing Candy Mountain database, Candy Mountain has no cap-* or plugin-* folder, starts on that database without applying a migration, and every feature works as before. Change a label in one capability in the capabilities checkout, see it in Candy Mountain through a link without publishing, then push it and see the new version in the registry a few minutes later without opening a pull request. In a freshly generated product, add one capability with one command and see its page in the running app.

title: Base: linking a product that has its own capability packages loads drizzle-orm, hono and typescript-eslint twice
description: Context: base repo crab-shack/platform (checkout /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/platform; phase-3 work uncommitted in worktree /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/platform-phase3). A product is pointed at a local base checkout with pnpm platform-link and back with pnpm platform-unlink (docs/linking.md in the base); linked packages resolve their own dependencies from the checkout's node_modules. Problem (found by 8by.4.8 while verifying the product generator, 2026-11-10): in a product that has its own capability packages (any generated product; Candy Mountain), after platform-link the capability package's typecheck fails because drizzle-orm and hono types load twice (one copy from the checkout's node_modules via the linked platform packages, one from the product's), and the web app's lint fails with 'Different instances of plugin @typescript-eslint'. Install and other packages' lint pass. Verification of 8by.4.8 therefore used packed tarballs instead of linking. This breaks the cross-repo development loop phase 2 built for exactly such products. What to build: make a linked product's gates behave as they do on the registry version, e.g. by having the link make the linked platform packages resolve shared peer libraries (drizzle-orm, hono, typescript-eslint and whatever else the check reveals) from the product, or by declaring them as peer dependencies of the platform packages so pnpm dedupes, whichever is sound for published packages too; justify the choice. Reproduce first with a product generated by 'platform-new product' into a temp dir outside both repos and linked to the checkout. Non-goals: no change to the unlinked/registry behaviour beyond what the fix needs. Update docs/linking.md if behaviour changes. Changeset as CONTRIBUTING.md requires. Gates: pnpm lint, typecheck (serial), test, build green in the base, and the linked generated product's four gates green (lint through turbo without the platform-check-linked guard, which correctly refuses a linked state). Do not commit unless the assigner says so.
acceptance_criteria: A product generated by platform-new product and linked to the base checkout passes typecheck, test, build and turbo lint while linked; unlinking returns it to the registry state with nothing left behind; docs/linking.md reflects any change; changeset present; four base gates green.
close_reason: Fixed in shared worktree (uncommitted): platform-link adds major-scoped pnpm overrides pointing libraries shared by the product and the linked platform packages (vue, hono, drizzle-orm, typescript-eslint via @nuxt/eslint, ...) at the checkout's node_modules symlinks, recorded in state.json so unlink removes them; manifests exported from check; docs/linking.md; .changeset/link-shared-libraries.md (patch). Linked generated product passes typecheck/lint/test/build; unlink restores byte for byte. Peers could not fix it (link: resolves peers from the checkout).

title: Base: the per-major page records the SDK-major declaration, and the author entry page links the connection guide
description: Context: base repo crab-shack/platform, phase 3 work uncommitted in the shared worktree /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/platform-phase3. The docs bead 8by.4.10 added docs/capability-majors.md (the page that holds, per major version, what a capability author must change to cross it, with the rule that the PR carrying a major changeset adds the entry under '## <next major>.0.0') and docs/capability-authors.md (the entry page for capability authors). Two major changesets are in the tree without an entry on the majors page: .changeset/daemon-sdk-major.md (8by.4.1: a capability states the SDK major it targets as a peerDependency on @crab-shack/platform-sdk naming one major, e.g. "0.x", plus package and sdkMajor fields on its definition; the daemon refuses a mismatch or a missing statement at boot; a drift check capabilitySdkDrift in platform-config's package-boundaries reports package.json vs definition disagreement) and .changeset/web-layer-sdk-major.md (8by.4.2: the web layer list fails the build for a layer package whose peer range names another major or none). And the worked connection package packages/plugin-sample (8by.4.6), whose README is the connection author's guide, has no row on the entry page. What to build: add the entry for those two changesets to docs/capability-majors.md following the page's own rule and entry shape, under the heading the rule gives for the next major (changesets turns a major bump of 0.4.x into 1.0.0; Jack decides the actual number at release, so add one short line in the entry or the release bead notes saying the heading follows the released number). The entry tells a capability author exactly what to add, derived from the two changesets and docs/upgrade-path.md; keep it consistent with them, do not invent. Add a row or line for the connection author's guide (packages/plugin-sample/README.md, by GitHub URL as the page does for the template guide) to docs/capability-authors.md. Non-goals: no code change; do not touch other sections. Other agents work in the same tree: re-read before editing, small local edits, never commit/stash/reset. A patch changeset is not needed unless a published package's README changes. Gates: pnpm lint and every relative link in changed docs resolves.
acceptance_criteria: docs/capability-majors.md has an entry for the SDK-major declaration that says what a capability author must add (both halves) and follows the page's rule; docs/capability-authors.md links the connection author's guide; changed links resolve; lint green.
close_reason: Done in shared worktree (uncommitted): docs/capability-majors.md '## 1.0.0' entry for the SDK-major declaration (both halves, drift check, link to upgrade-path); docs/capability-authors.md links the connection author's guide (relative + GitHub URL). Lint green.

title: Rehearse the phase 3 human test on the released version and hand Jack the checklist
description:
Context: two repositories on this machine. The base (github.com/crab-shack/platform, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/platform; other git worktrees of it may sit beside it) is a pnpm 12 workspace run through Turborepo that holds the platform: packages/platform-daemon (a Hono daemon over SQLite via Drizzle: database and migrations, secrets, auth, workspaces, registries, grants, threads, the platform agent, startPlatform, createApp, runDaemon, and a /testing entry that is the test kit a capability's daemon tests import), packages/platform-web (the web shell as a Nuxt layer package, with the contribution points, the layer-list helpers a web app's Nuxt config calls with the product's layer ids, the cm-layers lint and a /test kit), packages/platform-sdk (wire types and the product configuration type on a Node-free root entry; defineCapabilityDefinition and the capability contract on the /daemon entry), packages/platform-config (address and data-directory resolution, the tsconfig, ESLint and vitest presets every package extends, the cm-packages boundary lint and its package-boundaries helpers, and the platform-link, platform-unlink and platform-check-linked commands a product runs) and packages/platform-cli (start, stop, status, logs, install-service for a distribution). These five are published together at one shared version (a Changesets fixed group; 0.3.1 at the time of writing) to GitHub Packages as private @crab-shack/platform-* packages: the daemon-side ones as built output, platform-web as source. Beside them: packages/cap-template (id template, private and never published: the deliberately small capability that exercises every contribution point and is the worked example an author copies; its README is the capability author's guide) and apps/, the base's own development distribution (apps/product, a plain-data product package; apps/daemon; apps/web) that runs the platform with the template and is what the base's tests boot. The READMEs of platform-daemon and platform-web are the conventions documents for a capability's daemon half and web half; docs/ holds registry-access.md, linking.md and upgrade-path.md; CONTRIBUTING.md holds the changeset rule.

Candy Mountain (github.com/kingrea/candy-mountain-v3, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/candy-mountain-v3, where this bead tracker lives) is a product built on the base: capability packages under its own scope @candy-mountain/ (packages/cap-<id>, feature capabilities with a manifest; packages/plugin-<id>, connection packages, each service-only and bringing the one plugin type its id names), a plain-data product package (packages/candy-mountain) and thin apps (apps/daemon lists every capability definition and runs runDaemon over the product; apps/web extends platform-web and the capability layers; apps/cli). It installs the five platform packages from the registry pinned at one exact version (0.3.0 at the time of writing) in every package.json. A product is pointed at a local base checkout with pnpm platform-link and back with pnpm platform-unlink (docs/linking.md in the base); a linked state is never left behind or committed.

A capability is one package with a daemon half (a definition made with defineCapabilityDefinition, exported from the package's root entry as a factory) and, when it has UI, a web half (a Nuxt layer at the package root, declared by a webLayer id in its package.json). The daemon boots a product: plain-data product configuration (name, description, theme, scope label and URL prefix, and the id lists of capabilities, modules, plugin types and layers) joined with the capability definitions and module definitions, and it refuses to boot, naming the offender, when they disagree.

This bead belongs to the phase of the platform-package work whose goal is that a capability built for the wrong SDK major is refused with a clear message, a capability's product-level settings are declared and checked at boot, a product can be described by one file, and a new capability or a new product starts from a generator instead of a blank directory. Standing decisions, not to revisit: packages are private and never public; the five platform packages share one version line and semver is meant; capabilities stay unpublished workspace packages inside each product, under the product's own scope; a defect in the base is fixed in the base and released, never worked around in a product.

Working rules: the gates are pnpm lint, pnpm typecheck (serial on purpose; parallel typechecks are killed for memory on this machine, so never raise its concurrency), pnpm test and pnpm build, green in every repository the bead touches. Other agents may be working in the same checkouts and running installs and gates at the same time; follow whatever locking and branch arrangement the person who assigned this bead gave you. A change to a published platform package carries a changeset as the base's CONTRIBUTING.md describes. Do not commit, push, or open or merge pull requests in either repository unless whoever assigned this bead tells you to; otherwise leave the work in the working tree and report the changed files. Work this bead depends on may not be on the base's main branch yet; whoever assigned the bead tells you where it is.

Problem: the phase ends with a human test Jack runs by hand. Everything it exercises was built and checked piece by piece against local checkouts, before the release existed. Nobody has yet run the whole path the way a product owner will: from the registry, with nothing linked. Whatever is broken on that path should be found, and filed, before Jack spends an afternoon on it.

The human test, verbatim: generate a capability into Candy Mountain, add it to both apps and see it running. Change its declared SDK major and confirm the daemon refuses to start naming it, and the web build fails naming it. Generate a product distribution into an empty directory, add one generated capability, run its pipeline and start it with the placeholder name and the capability's page showing. Put a wrong value for one of its settings in the product file and confirm the daemon refuses to start naming the capability and the key; put a right value and confirm the capability sees it.

What to do, using only the released version from the registry (it is in the notes of the release bead this one depends on) and never a linked checkout:
- In a throwaway copy of Candy Mountain, so the real checkout is untouched, run the first two sentences of the test for a feature capability. Also generate a connection package there and confirm its own checks pass.
- In an empty directory outside any repository, run the rest of the test with the product generator. This machine's user-level npm configuration already holds the registry token.
- For each step that fails, work out whose defect it is. A defect in the base is filed as a bug bead under this bead's parent epic with a reproduction, and is not worked around in a product, because the fix needs a base release. A wrong sentence in a document may be corrected in the base's working tree directly.
- Write the checklist Jack will follow: for each sentence of the human test, the exact commands and what he should see. Put it in this bead's notes with, for each step, either the evidence that it passed (the command and the line observed) or the id of the bead filed for it.
- Remove the throwaway directories and stop anything left listening on a port.

Non-goals: do not fix base defects here beyond documentation; do not leave a generated capability or any other change in Candy Mountain's real checkout; do not commit anywhere.
acceptance_criteria: This bead's notes hold, for every sentence of the human test, the exact commands and either the observed evidence that the step passed on the registry version or the id of a bug bead filed for it. The checklist is complete enough for Jack to run the test without reading anything else. Candy Mountain's real checkout shows no change from this bead in git status, and the throwaway directories are gone.
notes: Orchestrator note (2026-11-10): 8by.4.5's Candy Mountain acceptance check (generated @candy-mountain/cap-<id> passes its own lint/typecheck/tests) was deferred to this rehearsal because CM could not link to the phase-3 checkout before adopting the SDK-major declaration. Verify it explicitly here: pnpm platform-new capability <id> <label> in CM, pnpm install, the new package's own checks pass untouched.

Problem: Candy Mountain's bots capability reads three tuning values (the maximum worktrees per project, the idle timeout after which a worktree lease is reclaimed, and the reclaim interval) from the environment variables CM_WORKTREES_PER_PROJECT, CM_WORKTREE_IDLE_TIMEOUT and CM_WORKTREE_RECLAIM_INTERVAL, deep inside the capability, and checks them only when that code runs. The platform version Candy Mountain is now on lets a capability declare its product-level settings and have the daemon validate them at boot, naming the capability and the key when one is wrong. Bots is the first real capability to move, which proves the mechanism outside the base's template and gives these values one declared home.

What to build, in Candy Mountain: the bots capability declares these three settings with their current defaults (4, two hours, ten minutes) and receives them validated through its start context; the product supplies them in code. Existing deployments must behave identically: the three environment variables keep their names, keep accepting the formats they accept today (a positive integer; durations such as 90s, 15m or 2h up to thirty days) and still override the product's values. Where the environment is read is yours to choose, as long as the capability's internals no longer reach for it. A bad value now stops the daemon at boot with a message naming bots and the key. Say in Candy Mountain's documentation of its settings where these now live.

Defaults and non-goals: the code options the bots factory takes for tests (a fake worktree pool and the like) stay a code seam. Do not convert any other capability. Do not move Candy Mountain to a product file. Do not change what the settings do.
acceptance_criteria: The bots capability declares the three settings with the same defaults as before and reads them only through the declared mechanism. With no environment variables set the daemon starts with those defaults; each environment variable still overrides its value with the same accepted formats. A wrong value, from the product or from an environment variable, stops the daemon at boot with a message naming bots and the key. The existing worktree tests pass with their intent unchanged. The four gates are green in Candy Mountain. Nothing is committed.
notes: Done in working tree (uncommitted). For the move of bots to @crab-shack/cap-bots: (1) Declared: BOTS_SETTINGS in packages/cap-bots/src/worktrees/config.ts (keys worktreesPerProject int>=1 default 4; worktreeIdleTimeoutMs and worktreeReclaimIntervalMs ints 1..2592000000 ms, defaults 7200000 and 600000), exported with BotsSettings, worktreeSettings(), DEFAULT_WORKTREE_SETTINGS; botsDefinition sets settings: BOTS_SETTINGS and reads context.settings in start (options.worktrees still override, test seam only). The package reads no environment and knows no CM_* name; it can move as is. (2) Environment: read only in Candy Mountain, apps/daemon/src/settings.ts candyMountainSettings(env) (CM_WORKTREES_PER_PROJECT, CM_WORKTREE_IDLE_TIMEOUT, CM_WORKTREE_RECLAIM_INTERVAL, old formats, checked with settingValueProblem against BOTS_SETTINGS, ProductError naming bots/key/variable); index.ts passes process.env via candyMountainProduct({}, process.env); tests get no env. It imports BOTS_SETTINGS from @candy-mountain/cap-bots: repoint that import after the rename. (3) A product supplies a bots block in Product.settings (Candy Mountain: CANDY_MOUNTAIN_SETTINGS in packages/candy-mountain/src/settings.ts) or nothing to take the defaults; the platform refuses a bots block when bots is not listed, so apps/daemon/src/testing/platform.ts candyMountainWith filters settings blocks to the capabilities kept. Docs: apps/daemon/README.md 'Product settings'.
close_reason: Bots declares worktreesPerProject, worktreeIdleTimeoutMs, worktreeReclaimIntervalMs (BOTS_SETTINGS in cap-bots worktrees/config.ts); product supplies them in packages/candy-mountain/src/settings.ts; CM_WORKTREE* env read only in apps/daemon/src/settings.ts and still overrides. Four gates green. Uncommitted.

title: Release the base with the phase 3 contract and record the version
description:
This bead is Jack's: agents cannot merge pull requests on crab-shack/platform or publish.

Why it exists: the base work of this phase (the SDK major check in the daemon and the web build, declared capability settings, the product file, the two generators, the worked connection package and the conventions) reaches products only through a release. Candy Mountain's adoption and the rehearsal of the phase's human test wait on the version this produces.

What to do: land every finished phase 3 change on the base's main branch, merge the Version Packages pull request the release workflow opens, and confirm the platform packages (and any package the generators added to the shared version line) are on the organisation's packages page at the new version.

One decision to make here. The SDK major check is a breaking change for every existing capability, so its changesets are written as breaking and Changesets will propose 1.0.0. That is the natural moment for it: the check compares semver majors, every 0.x version is major 0, so on a 0.x line the check can never fire between two platform releases. If you would rather stay on 0.x for now, lower those changesets to minor before merging, knowing a breaking 0.x minor will not be caught by the check.

Then record the released version in this bead's notes; the beads that depend on this one read it there.
acceptance_criteria: The platform packages are published at one new version that contains the phase 3 base work, and that version is written in this bead's notes together with the choice made about 1.0.0.
notes:
Orchestrator note (2026-11-10): if the release is numbered 1.0.0, change packages/cap-template and packages/plugin-sample peer range "0.x" and sdkMajor: 0 to major 1 in the same release, or the base dev distribution refuses to boot and the web build fails. SDK_VERSION is synced from package.json by scripts/sync-sdk-version.mjs in the root version-packages script.
Orchestrator note from 8by.4.10 (2026-11-10), for Jack's ruling — left as NOT promised in the contract sections: (1) test kits platform-daemon/testing, platform-web/test and /test/vitest (but upgrade-path.md implies stable); (2) daemon root exports used by distributions (startPlatform, createApp, runDaemon, loadDaemonConfig, boot-time auth/secrets/notification/data-dir/db functions, registry constructors, startCapabilities, migrationSets, assertProduct etc.) — CONTRIBUTING calls breaking anything a product consumes a major; (3) platform definitions and their ids/tools (THREADS_CAPABILITY_ID, SESSION_FAMILIES are imported by Candy Mountain); (4) SDK names re-exported by the daemon root (CM imports definePluginType and CapabilityDefinitionError from the daemon root 8x each); (5) web: unnamed auto-imports (useProjects, usePlugins, useChatPanel), shell pages/markup/classes/token values, generated route names, files not in exports, error/lint wording; layer app-config keys left out of contribution points. Promised by the agent's own reading (confirm): daemon root groups from 'Route helpers and gates' onward incl. setGrant/setEnabledModules/workspace create-archive-delete; /layer-list; a lint rule refusing previously accepted code is a major. Guide reach: READMEs link GitHub URLs; readers with registry access but no repo read access cannot open the guide.
Orchestrator note (8by.4.16): docs/capability-majors.md has a '## 1.0.0' entry whose snippets show "0.x"/sdkMajor: 0 with prose saying write 1.x/sdkMajor: 1 for the 1.0.0 platform. At release: rename the heading if the number differs, and if it is 1.0.0 change the snippets to "1.x" and sdkMajor: 1 along with cap-template and plugin-sample.

2026-11-11 decision (Jack): stay on 0.x until the platform is fully released and in use by the team. The phase 3 release is 0.5.0, not 1.0.0. Branch release-stay-0x (platform repo, off main after PR #13): the two major changesets are now minor; CONTRIBUTING, upgrade-path, capability-majors (section is now 0.5.0) and both READMEs' contract sections say that before 1.0.0 a breaking change ships as a minor with the same duties as a major; scripts/sync-sdk-version.mjs puts every packages/* SDK peer range back to <major>.x after changeset version (changesets rewrote 0.x to the exact version). Simulated pnpm version-packages -> 0.5.0, then lint, typecheck, test (9/9) and build all passed. Release PR #14 as currently generated would publish 1.0.0 and fails CI: do not merge it until release-stay-0x lands, after which the changesets action regenerates it at 0.5.0. Template, plugin-sample and docs samples stay on major 0.
close_reason: Released 0.5.0 (tag v0.5.0, release workflow green on merge of #14). Stayed on 0.x per Jack; #15 made the breaking changesets minor and fixed peer-range rewriting in sync-sdk-version.mjs.
