title: Base: the conventions documents state the contract a capability author can rely on
description:

These five are published together at one shared version (a Changesets fixed group; 0.3.1 at the time of writing) to GitHub Packages as private @crab-shack/platform-* packages: the daemon-side ones as built output, platform-web as source. Beside them: packages/cap-template (id template, private and never published: the deliberately small capability that exercises every contribution point and is the worked example an author copies; its README is the capability author's guide) and apps/, the base's own development distribution (apps/product, a plain-data product package; apps/daemon; apps/web) that runs the platform with the template and is what the base's tests boot. A product is pointed at a local base checkout with pnpm platform-link and back with pnpm platform-unlink (docs/linking.md in the base); a linked state is never left behind or committed.

The daemon boots a product: plain-data product configuration (name, description, theme, scope label and URL prefix, and the id lists of capabilities, modules, plugin types and layers) joined with the capability definitions and module definitions, and it refuses to boot, naming the offender, when they disagree.

A change to a published platform package carries a changeset as the base's CONTRIBUTING.md describes. Do not commit, push, or open or merge pull requests in either repository unless whoever assigned this bead tells you to; otherwise leave the work in the working tree and report the changed files. Work this bead depends on may not be on the base's main branch yet; whoever assigned the bead tells you where it is.

Problem: the conventions are the contract between the platform and every capability, and that matters now that capabilities live in other repositories and cross platform releases. Today the contract is three READMEs written while everything lived inside Candy Mountain. The daemon conventions' section on what the platform keeps stable opens by saying nothing is versioned yet and points at a plan file in another repository. The web conventions have no statement of what stays stable at all. Some wording still assumes the reader is inside Candy Mountain or that a workspace is a project. There is no single place an author starts from. An author working in a product repository cannot read the capability author's guide at all, because it is the README of a package that is never published. And although CONTRIBUTING.md requires a breaking changeset to say what a capability author must change, there is no page where an author reads those instructions major by major.

What to build, in the base:
- An entry point for capability authors in the base's docs that links the daemon conventions, the web conventions, the author's guide, the two test kits and the pages on registry access, linking and upgrading. Someone who has only the installed packages, or only access to the repository, must be able to reach every one of them; decide how the author's guide reaches such a reader.
- In each of the daemon and web conventions, one findable place that states four things: the directions in which a capability may import, the contribution points it may use, what the platform promises to keep stable across minor releases, and what it does not promise. The daemon document has most of this and needs bringing up to date for a published platform; the web document needs it written. Derive the promises from what the packages actually export and enforce. Do not invent a promise: where you cannot tell whether something is meant to be stable, list it as not promised and name it in the handoff for Jack to rule on.
- Wording that assumes the reader is in Candy Mountain, that nothing is published, or that points at files outside the base, corrected. Candy Mountain may remain as a named example of a product.
- A page that holds, for every major version, what a capability author must change to cross it, with the rule for adding to it, linked from docs/upgrade-path.md and CONTRIBUTING.md. It starts with its structure and the rule; releases fill it.

Defaults and non-goals: this is documentation only, with no code change. Do not rewrite the how-to content of the conventions. Do not document the features other beads are adding at the same time (the SDK major check, declared settings, the product file, the generators); each documents itself, so leave such sections alone if they appear while you work. A README inside a published package is part of that package, so follow CONTRIBUTING.md on changesets (a patch).
acceptance_criteria: The base's docs have an author entry page, linked from the root README, from which the daemon conventions, web conventions, author's guide, both test kits and the registry, linking and upgrade pages are each one link away, and the author's guide is reachable by a reader without a base checkout. The daemon and the web conventions each state the import directions, the usable contribution points, what is stable across minors and what is not. No document in the base says nothing is versioned yet, points at a file outside the base, or addresses the reader as being inside Candy Mountain. A per-major page for capability authors exists and is linked from docs/upgrade-path.md and CONTRIBUTING.md. Every relative link in the changed documents resolves. The handoff lists anything left as not promised for Jack's ruling. The four gates are green in the base.
close_reason: Done in shared worktree crab-shack/platform-phase3 (uncommitted, docs only): docs/capability-authors.md entry page; docs/capability-majors.md per-major page (rule + empty); '## The contract' sections (import directions, contribution points, stable across minors, not promised) in platform-daemon and platform-web READMEs; Candy Mountain/unversioned wording fixed; links from README, CONTRIBUTING, upgrade-path; .changeset/conventions-contract.md (patch). Not-promised list for Jack recorded on 8by.4.11 notes.

title: Base: a worked connection package beside the template
description:
Context: two repositories on this machine. The base (github.com/crab-shack/platform, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/platform; other git worktrees of it may sit beside it) is a pnpm 12 workspace run through Turborepo that holds the platform: packages/platform-daemon (a Hono daemon over SQLite via Drizzle: database and migrations, secrets, auth, workspaces, registries, grants, threads, the platform agent, startPlatform, createApp, runDaemon, and a /testing entry that is the test kit a capability's daemon tests import), packages/platform-web (the web shell as a Nuxt layer package, with the contribution points, the layer-list helpers a web app's Nuxt config calls with the product's layer ids, the cm-layers lint and a /test kit), packages/platform-sdk (wire types and the product configuration type on a Node-free root entry; defineCapabilityDefinition and the capability contract on the /daemon entry), packages/platform-config (address and data-directory resolution, the tsconfig, ESLint and vitest presets every package extends, the cm-packages boundary lint and its package-boundaries helpers, and the platform-link, platform-unlink and platform-check-linked commands a product runs) and packages/platform-cli (start, stop, status, logs, install-service for a distribution). These five are published together at one shared version (a Changesets fixed group; 0.3.1 at the time of writing) to GitHub Packages as private @crab-shack/platform-* packages: the daemon-side ones as built output, platform-web as source. Beside them: packages/cap-template (id template, private and never published: the deliberately small capability that exercises every contribution point and is the worked example an author copies; its README is the capability author's guide) and apps/, the base's own development distribution (apps/product, a plain-data product package; apps/daemon; apps/web) that runs the platform with the template and is what the base's tests boot. The READMEs of platform-daemon and platform-web are the conventions documents for a capability's daemon half and web half; docs/ holds registry-access.md, linking.md and upgrade-path.md; CONTRIBUTING.md holds the changeset rule.

Candy Mountain (github.com/kingrea/candy-mountain-v3, checkout at /home/kingrea/work/candy-mountain-v3, where this bead tracker lives) is a product built on the base: capability packages under its own scope @candy-mountain/ (packages/cap-<id>, feature capabilities with a manifest; packages/plugin-<id>, connection packages, each service-only and bringing the one plugin type its id names), a plain-data product package (packages/candy-mountain) and thin apps (apps/daemon lists every capability definition and runs runDaemon over the product; apps/web extends platform-web and the capability layers; apps/cli). It installs the five platform packages from the registry pinned at one exact version (0.3.0 at the time of writing) in every package.json. A product is pointed at a local base checkout with pnpm platform-link and back with pnpm platform-unlink (docs/linking.md in the base); a linked state is never left behind or committed.

A capability is one package with a daemon half (a definition made with defineCapabilityDefinition, exported from the package's root entry as a factory) and, when it has UI, a web half (a Nuxt layer at the package root, declared by a webLayer id in its package.json). The daemon boots a product: plain-data product configuration (name, description, theme, scope label and URL prefix, and the id lists of capabilities, modules, plugin types and layers) joined with the capability definitions and module definitions, and it refuses to boot, naming the offender, when they disagree.

This bead belongs to the phase of the platform-package work whose goal is that a capability built for the wrong SDK major is refused with a clear message, a capability's product-level settings are declared and checked at boot, a product can be described by one file, and a new capability or a new product starts from a generator instead of a blank directory. Standing decisions, not to revisit: packages are private and never public; the five platform packages share one version line and semver is meant; capabilities stay unpublished workspace packages inside each product, under the product's own scope; a defect in the base is fixed in the base and released, never worked around in a product.

Working rules: the gates are pnpm lint, pnpm typecheck (serial on purpose; parallel typechecks are killed for memory on this machine, so never raise its concurrency), pnpm test and pnpm build, green in every repository the bead touches. Other agents may be working in the same checkouts and running installs and gates at the same time; follow whatever locking and branch arrangement the person who assigned this bead gave you. A change to a published platform package carries a changeset as the base's CONTRIBUTING.md describes. Do not commit, push, or open or merge pull requests in either repository unless whoever assigned this bead tells you to; otherwise leave the work in the working tree and report the changed files. Work this bead depends on may not be on the base's main branch yet; whoever assigned the bead tells you where it is.

Problem: a capability package comes in two shapes. A feature capability (cap-<id>) has a manifest and brings no plugin types. A connection package (plugin-<id>) is service-only: it has no manifest, its id is the id of the one plugin type it brings, and features that need the connection depend on it. The base has a worked example and an author's guide only for the first shape. Every existing connection package lives in Candy Mountain, which authors working on other products cannot see; the base's own tests never boot a product that brings a plugin type through a package; and the capability generator has nothing to derive the connection shape from.

What to build, in the base: a second small worked example, a connection package in packages/plugin-<id>, private, unpublished and ignored by Changesets exactly as the template is. Choose an id that is distinct from the template's and that survives the same mechanical renaming the template is put through, and use the template's five naming forms throughout. It brings one plugin type that exercises what a connection author actually uses: configuration fields, a secret, the test action, and whatever web contribution a plugin type has under the web conventions if it needs one. It talks to no real external service, so the base's tests need no network. Its tests use the test kit, including a plugin instance with fake secrets. Its README is the connection author's guide: short, stating the rules that make a package a connection package and pointing into the daemon conventions for the rest.

Include it in the base's development distribution so the base's tests boot it and the running distribution's plugins page offers it; the tests and documents that today say the distribution brings no plugin type, or runs the template alone, change to match. The template capability does not start requiring it: the feature example stays standalone. If, when you arrive, capability packages in the base state the SDK major they target or declare a settings shape, this package does the same (an empty settings shape); if not, the beads adding those will add them here. The development distribution may be partway through moving from a product package to a product file; add the new ids wherever the product is described when you arrive.

Non-goals: no generator support (a later bead), no real integration, no change to how plugin types work.
acceptance_criteria: The development distribution boots with the new plugin type registered, and the checks that hold capability packages to their kind (a plugin- package has no manifest and brings exactly the type its id names) pass with it included. In the running development distribution an admin can create an instance of the plugin type on a space, save its secret and run its test action successfully. The package's own lint, typecheck and tests pass on their own and need no network. Its README states the connection-package rules. The base README and the distribution's tests no longer claim the distribution brings no plugin type. The four gates are green in the base.
close_reason: Done in shared worktree crab-shack/platform-phase3 (uncommitted): packages/plugin-sample (id sample; workspace-scoped plugin type with account/region fields, token secret, health check; offline injected client; icon-only web layer), ignored by changesets; in dev distribution (product, daemon, web) with HTTP tests for create instance/save secret/test action; README is the connection author's guide; docs pointers + .changeset/plugin-sample-connection-guide.md (patch). All four gates green.

Problem: the platform is now published, and each product moves to a new version on its own schedule. A capability written against one major of the SDK and booted on another fails wherever the contract changed: at some call site, at run time, with an error that names neither the capability nor the cause. Nothing today records which SDK a capability was written for, so nothing can say so up front. Capabilities that live in client repositories only survive platform upgrades if a mismatch is caught at boot and named.

title: pnpm test: parallel vitest runs race on node_modules/.vitest-cache after an install changes dependencies
description: After a pnpm install that changes node_modules, the first pnpm test (turbo runs every package's vitest in parallel) fails several packages at startup with 'ENOTEMPTY: directory not empty, rmdir <repo>/node_modules/.vitest-cache': each vitest 5 process finds the shared cache stale and clears it, and the ones that lose the race exit before running a test. The second run passes. Seen twice during candy-mountain-v3-8by.3.1 (after installing @crab-shack/platform-* 0.1.0, and again after switching the override off), hitting plugin-heroku, plugin-repository, cap-acp, cap-issues, cap-uptime and plugin-claude-code at random. It is not caused by the platform switch (the vitest preset is unchanged), but it makes the test gate red on a fresh clone's first run. Fix in the base's vitest preset (definePackageTestConfig) if a per-package cacheDir removes the shared directory, otherwise in turbo.json or vitest's cache settings here; then confirm a fresh clone passes pnpm test on its first run. Acceptance: pnpm install followed by pnpm test is green on the first run, with only the known slack-notifications failures (candy-mountain-v3-5qz) if those are still open.
close_reason: Cause: vitest 5 fsModuleCache defaults to one cache at <workspace root>/node_modules/.vitest-cache; when the lockfile hash in its _metadata.json goes stale every parallel package vitest rm -rf's it at startup and the losers exit with ENOTEMPTY. Fix in the base preset (definePackageTestConfig sets fsModuleCachePath to the package's own node_modules/.vitest-cache), crab-shack/platform PR #10 with a patch changeset for @crab-shack/platform-config, not merged. Verified via platform-link: the reproduction went from 8/19 packages failing to 0, and a full parallel run with every per-package cache stale had no ENOTEMPTY. The product picks it up at the next platform release bump; until then the old shared cache still races.

title: Upgrade path page: what a product does when the base releases and what a changeset must say
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 (github.com/kingrea/candy-mountain-v3, "this repo" below) is a pnpm 12 workspace run through Turborepo (apps/*, packages/*; root scripts pnpm build, pnpm test, pnpm lint, pnpm typecheck, the last with --concurrency=1 because parallel typechecks are killed for memory on the development machine). Beside them: capability packages (packages/cap-<id> feature capabilities with a manifest; packages/plugin-<id> connection packages, each bringing one plugin type; each has a daemon definition on its root entry and, when it has UI, a Nuxt web layer at the package root with package.json "webLayer": "<id>"), packages/cap-template (id template: the deliberately small capability that exercises every contribution point, included in Candy Mountain only in development; its README is the capability author's guide), packages/claude-acp (the ACP shim; stays with Candy Mountain), the plain-data product package packages/candy-mountain (CANDY_MOUNTAIN_PRODUCT and the module definitions) and the thin apps (apps/daemon registers every definition in src/definitions.ts and runs runDaemon over the product; apps/web extends @candy-mountain/platform-web and depends on every layer package; apps/cli is the candy-mountain bin). Every package is private, version 0.0.0, named @candy-mountain/<name>, depends on siblings with workspace:* and exports TypeScript source (exports "." points at ./src/index.ts); lint, typecheck and test run against source with no prior build, which turbo.json relies on through its transit task; nothing is built for publishing and nothing is published anywhere. There is no CI workflow in this repo today. The SDK test kit and the daemon conventions document come from the platform-extraction plan's phase 5 (epic candy-mountain-v3-ncj.5) and the product theme contract (ProductTheme fields, the distribution-owned product stylesheet, the cm-layers styling rules) from the product-theme plan (epic candy-mountain-v3-i8n); both land before this work starts, so the platform you move already carries them.

This bead is part of the platform-package plan (.ai-docs/plans/platform-package/ in this repo): the platform packages (platform-daemon, platform-web, platform-sdk, platform-config, platform-cli), the template capability, the test kit and the conventions documents move to a separate base repository ("the base" below), get a name and a version, and are published to a private registry that Candy Mountain, a new home dashboard and later the digital hub install from. Decisions already made, not to revisit: the registry is GitHub Packages under the company's GitHub organisation, private, with consumers authenticating through a read-only token in their npm configuration locally and in CI (Verdaccio is the fallback only if token handling proves unworkable); versions are managed with Changesets, every platform package shares one version line and releases together, and semver is meant (a breaking SDK change is a major); packages are never public; capabilities stay unpublished workspace packages inside each product; the base must be runnable and testable on its own, with a development distribution that runs the platform with the template capability alone; the code moves with its git history by subtree split, with a plain copy acceptable only if the split fights back. The base's product name, npm scope, repository name and GitHub owner are Jack's to choose and are recorded in the notes of decision bead candy-mountain-v3-8by.1; read them there before starting and use them wherever this text says "the chosen scope" or @scope/. Gates: pnpm lint, pnpm --recursive --workspace-concurrency=1 typecheck, pnpm test and pnpm build green in every repository the bead touches. title: Changesets with one fixed version line across every platform package
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 (github.com/kingrea/candy-mountain-v3, "this repo" below) is a pnpm 12 workspace run through Turborepo (apps/*, packages/*; root scripts pnpm build, pnpm test, pnpm lint, pnpm typecheck, the last with --concurrency=1 because parallel typechecks are killed for memory on the development machine). It holds the platform packages: packages/platform-daemon (a Hono daemon over SQLite via Drizzle: database and migrations, secrets, auth, workspaces, registries, grants, threads, the platform agent, startPlatform, createApp, runDaemon; its README is the daemon conventions document), packages/platform-web (the web shell as a Nuxt layer package with the chat and overview layers, the contribution points, the layer-list helpers and the cm-layers lint; a playground/ directory its own lint, typecheck and tests run against; its README is the web conventions document and the theme contract), packages/platform-sdk (wire types and the product configuration type on the root entry, defineCapabilityDefinition and the capability contract on the /daemon entry, and the test kit entry a capability's tests import), packages/platform-config (address and data-directory resolution plus the tsconfig, ESLint and vitest presets every package extends, and the cm-packages boundary lint in eslint/package-boundaries.mjs, which keys package kinds on the @candy-mountain/platform-, cap- and plugin- name prefixes) and packages/platform-cli (start/stop/status/logs/install-service, taking the product and the apps' paths from a distribution). Beside them: capability packages (packages/cap-<id> feature capabilities with a manifest; packages/plugin-<id> connection packages, each bringing one plugin type; each has a daemon definition on its root entry and, when it has UI, a Nuxt web layer at the package root with package.json "webLayer": "<id>"), packages/cap-template (id template: the deliberately small capability that exercises every contribution point, included in Candy Mountain only in development; its README is the capability author's guide), packages/claude-acp (the ACP shim; stays with Candy Mountain), the plain-data product package packages/candy-mountain (CANDY_MOUNTAIN_PRODUCT and the module definitions) and the thin apps (apps/daemon registers every definition in src/definitions.ts and runs runDaemon over the product; apps/web extends @candy-mountain/platform-web and depends on every layer package; apps/cli is the candy-mountain bin). Every package is private, version 0.0.0, named @candy-mountain/<name>, depends on siblings with workspace:* and exports TypeScript source (exports "." points at ./src/index.ts); lint, typecheck and test run against source with no prior build, which turbo.json relies on through its transit task; nothing is built for publishing and nothing is published anywhere. There is no CI workflow in this repo today. The SDK test kit and the daemon conventions document come from the platform-extraction plan's phase 5 (epic candy-mountain-v3-ncj.5) and the product theme contract (ProductTheme fields, the distribution-owned product stylesheet, the cm-layers styling rules) from the product-theme plan (epic candy-mountain-v3-i8n); both land before this work starts, so the platform you move already carries them.

This bead is part of the platform-package plan (.ai-docs/plans/platform-package/ in this repo): the platform packages (platform-daemon, platform-web, platform-sdk, platform-config, platform-cli), the template capability, the test kit and the conventions documents move to a separate base repository ("the base" below), get a name and a version, and are published to a private registry that Candy Mountain, a new home dashboard and later the digital hub install from. Decisions already made, not to revisit: the registry is GitHub Packages under the company's GitHub organisation, private, with consumers authenticating through a read-only token in their npm configuration locally and in CI (Verdaccio is the fallback only if token handling proves unworkable); versions are managed with Changesets, every platform package shares one version line and releases together, and semver is meant (a breaking SDK change is a major); packages are never public; capabilities stay unpublished workspace packages inside each product; the base must be runnable and testable on its own, with a development distribution that runs the platform with the template capability alone; the code moves with its git history by subtree split, with a plain copy acceptable only if the split fights back. The base's product name, npm scope, repository name and GitHub owner are Jack's to choose and are recorded in the notes of decision bead candy-mountain-v3-8by.1; read them there before starting and use them wherever this text says "the chosen scope" or @scope/. Gates: pnpm lint, pnpm --recursive --workspace-concurrency=1 typecheck, pnpm test and pnpm build green in every repository the bead touches. Do not commit in this repo; in the base, commit on a branch and open a pull request only if the bead says so, otherwise leave the work in the working tree and report it.


Problem: the platform packages have no version and no changelog, so a consumer cannot pin a release or read what changed, and five packages that always change together would be bookkeeping if versioned independently.

What to build: add Changesets to the base, configured so every platform package (platform-daemon, platform-web, platform-sdk, platform-config, platform-cli) is in one fixed group sharing a single version line, with restricted access, the default branch as the base branch, and a changelog generated per package. The template capability and the development distribution are ignored by Changesets and never versioned or published. Add a changeset describing the initial release so the first version run gives every package the same first version. Document in the base's contributing notes that every change touching a platform package carries a changeset stating the bump level and, for a major, what a capability author must change. The version step must leave every platform package at the same version and update the dependency ranges between them accordingly.

Non-goals: no release workflow, no publishing, no build changes.

Acceptance: the changeset status command in the base lists the initial changeset against all five packages; running the version command locally and then discarding the result bumps all five to the same version and writes a changelog entry in each; the template capability and the distribution apps are untouched by it.
close_reason: Changesets configured (fixed group of 5, restricted, main), initial minor changeset, CONTRIBUTING.md; verified status and dry version run; commit on bead-2.5

Decisions already made, not to revisit: the registry is GitHub Packages under the company's GitHub organisation, private, with consumers authenticating through a read-only token in their npm configuration locally and in CI (Verdaccio is the fallback only if token handling proves unworkable); versions are managed with Changesets, every platform package shares one version line and releases together, and semver is meant (a breaking SDK change is a major); packages are never public; capabilities stay unpublished workspace packages inside each product; the base must be runnable and testable on its own, with a development distribution that runs the platform with the template capability alone; the code moves with its git history by subtree split, with a plain copy acceptable only if the split fights back. The base's product name, npm scope, repository name and GitHub owner are Jack's to choose and are recorded in the notes of decision bead candy-mountain-v3-8by.1; read them there before starting and use them wherever this text says "the chosen scope" or @scope/. Gates: pnpm lint, pnpm --recursive --workspace-concurrency=1 typecheck, pnpm test and pnpm build green in every repository the bead touches. Do not commit in this repo; in the base, commit on a branch and open a pull request only if the bead says so, otherwise leave the work in the working tree and report it.


Problem: nothing publishes the platform. A release must be one action the whole team can trust: pipeline green, every package at one version, private to the organisation, with types.

What to build: a release workflow in the base, built on the CI workflow, using the Changesets action on the default branch: when unreleased changesets exist it opens or updates a version pull request; when that pull request merges it builds and publishes every platform package in the fixed group to GitHub Packages under the organisation at the shared version, with restricted access, and tags the release. Publishing runs only after lint, typecheck, test and build are green in the same run. The workflow authenticates with the token GitHub grants to workflows, given package write permission, so no personal token is stored; if the organisation's settings make that impossible, say so in the handoff and use an organisation secret. Document in the base README how a release happens: write a changeset, merge, merge the version pull request, see the packages on the organisation's packages page. Cut the first release with it.

Non-goals: no consumer-side changes, no prerelease channels, no provenance.

Acceptance: the organisation's packages page lists the five platform packages at the same version, private, each tarball containing what the publishable-shape bead defines; a machine outside the base with a read-only token installs one of them by version; the base carries a tag for the version; a second changeset merged afterwards produces a new version pull request with no manual step.
notes:
Release workflow built and committed in the base (crab-shack/platform main, commit 9486ffd): .github/workflows/release.yml, root script release = pnpm build && changeset publish, README Releasing section (between <!-- releasing:start/end -->), docs/registry-access.md CI example corrected (pnpm 12.15.0 does not expand ${VAR} inside pnpm_config__auth; verified against a local fake registry; it now uses setup-node registry-url + NODE_AUTH_TOKEN, which pnpm and npm both honour). Nothing pushed or published. Local checks: YAML parses; changeset status lists all five minor; dry pnpm version-packages took the five to 0.1.0 with CHANGELOG.md each, cap-template/apps stayed 0.0.0, lockfile still frozen-valid, then discarded; pnpm build + pack of the non-private packages gives exactly five tarballs (note: plain pnpm -r pack also packs the four private ones, 9 tarballs; changeset publish skips private/ignored packages); lint, typecheck, test green.

STEPS FOR JACK (first release):
1. Org settings (github.com/organizations/crab-shack/settings): Actions > General > Workflow permissions: allow "Read and write permissions" (or at least do not force read-only, the workflow asks for contents/pull-requests/packages write) and tick "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests". Packages > Package creation: allow private packages. Same two Actions settings in the repo (crab-shack/platform Settings > Actions > General) if the org leaves them to repos.
2. Push: cd /home/kingrea/work/crab-shack/platform && git push -u origin main (branch upstream is currently "gone"; -u resets it). Ensure Actions is enabled for the repo.
3. Watch Actions: CI and Release both run on the push. Release runs the four gates, then the Changesets action opens PR "Version Packages" (branch changeset-release/main) bumping all five to 0.1.0 with CHANGELOGs and deleting .changeset/initial-release.md. CI does not run on that PR (opened by GITHUB_TOKEN); expected. If branch protection requires the CI check, close and reopen the PR or push an empty commit to its branch to trigger CI, or exempt it.
4. Merge the Version Packages PR. Release runs again: gates, pnpm release (build + changeset publish via pnpm publish to npm.pkg.github.com, access restricted), creates tags @crab-shack/platform-*@0.1.0 plus v0.1.0, pushes them.
5. Verify: github.com/orgs/crab-shack/packages lists platform-daemon, platform-web, platform-sdk, platform-config, platform-cli, each 0.1.0, Private, linked to crab-shack/platform. git fetch --tags && git tag shows v0.1.0 and the five per-package tags. Optionally inspect a tarball: pnpm pack @crab-shack/platform-sdk@0.1.0 on an authenticated machine, confirm dist/*.js + *.d.ts (platform-web: source).
6. Read-only install from another machine: create a classic PAT with only read:packages (SSO-authorise if enforced); in ~/.npmrc put //npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=<token>; in an empty dir: printf '@crab-shack:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com\n' > .npmrc; npm init -y (or a minimal package.json); pnpm add @crab-shack/platform-sdk@0.1.0. Expect success and node_modules/@crab-shack/platform-sdk/dist/index.d.ts present.
7. Second changeset: on a branch, pnpm changeset (patch, any platform package, e.g. a README line), commit, open PR, merge. Release run should open a new Version Packages PR bumping all five to 0.1.1 with no manual step. (Merging it would publish 0.1.1; optional.)

IF SOMETHING FAILS:
- Changesets action fails creating the PR ("GitHub Actions is not permitted to create or approve pull requests"): step 1 setting.
- Publish 403/401 (permission_denied, write_package): org forbids GITHUB_TOKEN package creation/write. Check Packages > Package creation; for an already-created package, Package settings > Manage Actions access > add crab-shack/platform with Write. Fallback: org owner makes a classic PAT with write:packages, stores as org secret CRAB_SHACK_PACKAGES_WRITE_TOKEN scoped to this repo, and in release.yml sets the release step's NODE_AUTH_TOKEN to ${{ secrets.CRAB_SHACK_PACKAGES_WRITE_TOKEN }} (keep GITHUB_TOKEN). Documented in README Releasing.
- Publish 404 / "not found" on pnpm info is normal for the first publish (changesets treats it as unpublished); a 404 on PUT means auth/scope: check the job log for the setup-node .npmrc and that NODE_AUTH_TOKEN is set on the action step.
- Partial publish (some of five published): rerun the failed job; changeset publish skips versions already in the registry and tags the rest.
- Tags missing but packages published: the action v1 may not parse changesets v3 output (published=false, no GitHub Releases); the "Tag the version" step pushes tags itself if the per-package sdk tag was created in the run. If absent, run locally on the release commit: git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin --tags (and pnpm changeset tag to recreate per-package tags).
- Install step fails on better-sqlite3 on Node 24: prebuild missing for the runner's ABI, it will compile from source (needs python/make, present on ubuntu-latest); if it fails, pin setup-node to the Node version used locally.
- Gates fail in Actions but pass locally: lockfile/pnpm 12 native binary download via pnpm/action-setup, or the root postinstall (nuxt prepare on the playground).
close_reason: Verified by Jack: Release workflow ran on GitHub, first release cut and working.

Problem: every platform package exports TypeScript source, which works for workspace siblings but not for a product in another repository: a consumer would need the base's TypeScript, presets and resolver configuration just to import a package. Everything a package reads at runtime or a consumer extends must be in the tarball: migration files, the tsconfig, ESLint and vitest presets, the boundary lint, and nothing else (no tests, no playground, no source maps pointing at files that are not shipped). The vitest preset is TypeScript today; a consumer must be able to extend it from node_modules. The web layer package (platform-web) publishes as source, the normal practice for a Nuxt layer compiled by the consumer's Nuxt: its nuxt.config, layers, app, server, modules, shared, the layer-list helpers and the cm-layers lint ship; its playground, tests and lint fixtures do not; and its postinstall must be harmless or absent when installed as a dependency. Every platform package declares the registry and restricted access in its publish configuration, drops the private flag, and keeps version 0.0.0 for Changesets to set. Peer dependencies are declared for what a consumer is expected to provide (Nuxt, Vue and Nuxt UI for the layer; vitest and ESLint for the config presets, already declared), with ranges matching what the base uses.

Non-goals: no publishing, no version bumps, no changes to the template capability (it is copied, not installed).

Acceptance: packing each platform package in the base produces a tarball whose file list contains built output with declarations (or source, for platform-web) and the runtime assets above and nothing from tests or playgrounds; installing those tarballs into a throwaway project outside the base, with no TypeScript configuration beyond extending the shipped preset, lets a script import the SDK's daemon entry, the daemon's root entry and the CLI, typecheck against the shipped declarations, and extend the ESLint and vitest presets; a Nuxt app in that project that extends the installed platform-web builds; the base's own gates stay green and still need no build before test.

It holds the platform packages: packages/platform-daemon (a Hono daemon over SQLite via Drizzle: database and migrations, secrets, auth, workspaces, registries, grants, threads, the platform agent, startPlatform, createApp, runDaemon; its README is the daemon conventions document), packages/platform-web (the web shell as a Nuxt layer package with the chat and overview layers, the contribution points, the layer-list helpers and the cm-layers lint; a playground/ directory its own lint, typecheck and tests run against; its README is the web conventions document and the theme contract), packages/platform-sdk (wire types and the product configuration type on the root entry, defineCapabilityDefinition and the capability contract on the /daemon entry, and the test kit entry a capability's tests import), packages/platform-config (address and data-directory resolution plus the tsconfig, ESLint and vitest presets every package extends, and the cm-packages boundary lint in eslint/package-boundaries.mjs, which keys package kinds on the @candy-mountain/platform-, cap- and plugin- name prefixes) and packages/platform-cli (start/stop/status/logs/install-service, taking the product and the apps' paths from a distribution). Beside them: capability packages (packages/cap-<id> feature capabilities with a manifest; packages/plugin-<id> connection packages, each bringing one plugin type; each has a daemon definition on its root entry and, when it has UI, a Nuxt web layer at the package root with package.json "webLayer": "<id>"), packages/cap-template (id template: the deliberately small capability that exercises every contribution point, included in Candy Mountain only in development; its README is the capability author's guide), packages/claude-acp (the ACP shim; stays with Candy Mountain), the plain-data product package packages/candy-mountain (CANDY_MOUNTAIN_PRODUCT and the module definitions) and the thin apps (apps/daemon registers every definition in src/definitions.ts and runs runDaemon over the product; apps/web extends @candy-mountain/platform-web and depends on every layer package; apps/cli is the candy-mountain bin). Every package is private, version 0.0.0, named @candy-mountain/<name>, depends on siblings with workspace:* and exports TypeScript source (exports "." points at ./src/index.ts); lint, typecheck and test run against source with no prior build, which turbo.json relies on through its transit task; nothing is built for publishing and nothing is published anywhere. There is no CI workflow in this repo today. The SDK test kit and the daemon conventions document come from the platform-extraction plan's phase 5 (epic candy-mountain-v3-ncj.5) and the product theme contract (ProductTheme fields, the distribution-owned product stylesheet, the cm-layers styling rules) from the product-theme plan (epic candy-mountain-v3-i8n); both land before this work starts, so the platform you move already carries them.

This bead is part of the platform-package plan (.ai-docs/plans/platform-package/ in this repo): the platform packages (platform-daemon, platform-web, platform-sdk, platform-config, platform-cli), the template capability, the test kit and the conventions documents move to a separate base repository ("the base" below), get a name and a version, and are published to a private registry that Candy Mountain, a new home dashboard and later the digital hub install from. Decisions already made, not to revisit: the registry is GitHub Packages under the company's GitHub organisation, private, with consumers authenticating through a read-only token in their npm configuration locally and in CI (Verdaccio is the fallback only if token handling proves unworkable); versions are managed with Changesets, every platform package shares one version line and releases together, and semver is meant (a breaking SDK change is a major); packages are never public; capabilities stay unpublished workspace packages inside each product; the base must be runnable and testable on its own, with a development distribution that runs the platform with the template capability alone; the code moves with its git history by subtree split, with a plain copy acceptable only if the split fights back. The base's product name, npm scope, repository name and GitHub owner are Jack's to choose and are recorded in the notes of decision bead candy-mountain-v3-8by.1; read them there before starting and use them wherever this text says "the chosen scope" or @scope/. Gates: pnpm lint, pnpm --recursive --workspace-concurrency=1 typecheck, pnpm test and pnpm build green in every repository the bead touches. Do not commit in this repo; in the base, commit on a branch and open a pull request only if the bead says so, otherwise leave the work in the working tree and report it.


Problem: the base has no CI, so nothing stops a broken change landing and the release workflow has no pipeline to build on.

What to build: a GitHub Actions workflow in the base that runs on every push to the default branch and every pull request: install with the pinned pnpm and a Node version the engines field allows, then lint, typecheck (one package at a time, as the root script already does), test and build, each a separate visible step, failing the run on the first red step. Cache the pnpm store between runs. The workflow needs no registry token, because the base installs only public dependencies and its own workspace packages. Document in the base README that CI runs the same four gates a developer runs.

Non-goals: no publishing, no release steps, no scheduled runs, no matrix across operating systems.

Acceptance: a pull request against the base shows the workflow with the four gates green; a commit that breaks a test makes the workflow fail on the test step and name the failing test in the log.
close_reason: Added .github/workflows/ci.yml (push to main + PRs; pnpm via packageManager, Node 24, store cache, frozen install, separate lint/typecheck/test/build steps) and a README CI section on branch bead-2.3. YAML parsed locally, pnpm lint green; actionlint unavailable. Live verification (green PR, failing test named in log) pending push.

Problem: after the move the base has packages but nothing that runs them. Without a distribution of its own, the base's tests have nothing to boot, a contributor cannot see a change, and nobody can tell whether the platform still quietly depends on a Candy Mountain capability.

What to build: a development distribution inside the base: a daemon entry and a web app, kept as thin as this repo's apps/daemon and apps/web, that assemble the platform with the template capability and nothing else, under the placeholder product name the decision bead's notes give and a plain product configuration with a scope label of its own. close_reason: Base dev distribution on crab-shack/platform branch bead-2.2: apps/product (@crab-shack/product), apps/daemon (@crab-shack/daemon), apps/web (@crab-shack/web) run the platform with the template alone; boot/product/schema/dependency-line tests and the web distribution test in the root pipeline; root pnpm dev starts both; README section added and conventions docs re-aimed.
