title: Phase 3: Compatibility contract and scaffold
description:
Capability: a capability built against the wrong SDK major is refused at boot with a clear message, and a new capability or a new product starts from a scaffold rather than a blank directory. Plan: .ai-docs/plans/platform-package/phase-3-compatibility-and-scaffold.md. Covers the compatibility check (each capability declares the SDK major it targets as a peer dependency and in its definition; the daemon refuses a mismatch at boot naming the package and both versions; the web build fails the same way through the layer list; the changelog states per major what an author must change), declared settings validated at boot, the product file (the product configuration, module list and a settings block per capability in one file), the capability generator in both shapes the connection-packages plan defines (cap- with a manifest, plugin- service-only bringing its plugin type), the product generator (a repo skeleton with the two thin apps, a product file, the pipeline, registry authentication and one generated capability), and the conventions documents and capability author's guide as the stated contract of what stays stable across minors.

Decomposed 2026-11-10 into 15 beads, 40 points. Since phase 2 the platform lives in the base repository (crab-shack/platform), so most of the work is there; Candy Mountain adopts it after a release.
- Base, no dependencies (seven ready at once): cjp declared settings (opus 3), 8by.4.1 daemon SDK-major check (opus 3), 8by.4.2 web build SDK-major check (opus 2), 8by.4.3 product file and reader (opus 3), 8by.4.5 capability generator (fable 4), 8by.4.6 worked connection package (opus 3), 8by.4.10 conventions as the contract (opus 3).
- Base, dependent: 8by.4.4 development distribution on a product file (opus 2; after cjp and 4.3), 8by.4.7 connection shape in the generator (opus 2; after 4.5 and 4.6), 8by.4.8 product generator (fable 4; after 4.4 and 4.5), 8by.4.9 CI workflow in the generated product (sonnet 2; after 4.8).
- 8by.4.11 release (Jack; after every base bead), then in Candy Mountain 8by.4.12 move to the release and state the SDK major in every capability package (opus 3), 8by.4.13 bots worktree limits as declared settings (opus 2), and 8by.4.14 rehearsal of the human test on the registry version with a checklist for Jack (opus 3).

Decisions baked into the beads: the SDK-major declaration is a peer dependency on @crab-shack/platform-sdk naming one major plus the same major on the definition, compared as semver majors with no special case for 0.x, and a capability with no declaration is refused (breaking, so the release bead carries the 1.0.0 choice). The generators have one source each: the capability generator derives from cap-template, the connection shape from a second worked example added to the base's development distribution, the product generator from the base's own apps; a generated capability therefore inherits the template's one example setting instead of an empty settings shape, which is what makes the last step of the human test runnable. The settings contract lands in the base (cjp was rewritten for that) and the bots conversion is a Candy Mountain bead after the release. Candy Mountain keeps its TypeScript product package; only the base's development distribution and generated products use the product file. The product file holds no secrets and no stylesheet path.

Human test: generate a capability into Candy Mountain, add it to both apps and see it running. Change its declared SDK major and confirm the daemon refuses to start naming it and the web build fails naming it. Generate a product distribution into an empty directory, add one generated capability, run its pipeline and start it with the placeholder name and the capability's page showing. Put a wrong value for one of its settings in the product file and confirm the daemon refuses to start naming the capability and the key; put a right value and confirm the capability sees it.

title: Phase 4: Home dashboard, the first single-scope product (not yet decomposed)
description:
Capability: a second product, built from the scaffold in its own repository, runs on the platform with a single workspace the user never sees, one capability of its own, and chat with a native agent. This is the proof that the base is a base. Plan: .ai-docs/plans/platform-package/phase-4-home-dashboard.md. Covers single-scope mode as product configuration (the daemon creates the default workspace at first boot and refuses a second while the mode is on; the shell hides the picker and the projects page, auto-selects the one workspace, redirects the root into it and never shows the scope label; module enablement, grants, plugin instances and the gate keep working; the URL prefix stays, with mounting scope pages at the root decided afterwards by looking at it), the home dashboard repository from the product scaffold (its own name, a brand colour outside Tailwind's palette, its own typeface and logo entirely from product configuration and stylesheet, password auth, the platform's standard pages) with one recipes capability from the capability scaffold (list and detail page, its own table, a has-recipes workspace fact, no plugin type, bare UI) and a native Mastra agent through the platform's native family with one tool that reads recipes so the chat rail and panel work with no ACP capability installed (Jack adds the LLM gateway key; the capability declares the platform fact it needs). Every assumption the base reveals (a page that says project, a composable expecting a picker, a registry field assuming a git repository) is fixed in the base and released, never worked around in the product.

Not yet decomposed: per the plan, decompose this phase when phase 2 closes, alongside phase 3, with the plan-decomposition-into-beads skill.

Human test: clone the home dashboard repo on a clean machine, install, start, log in, and land on the overview with no picker and no mention of projects or workspaces. Enable the recipes module, add a recipe, see it in the list and on the overview's fact. Open the chat rail, start a thread with the recipes agent and ask what is for dinner; it answers from the recipe table. Confirm the plugins page, grants page and settings all work. Then start Candy Mountain on the same base version and confirm it still shows its picker and projects unchanged.
notes:
Product repo for the home dashboard already exists: crab-shack/test-dashboard-home, cloned empty at ~/work/crab-shack/test-dashboard-home (as of 2026-11-09). Base repo is crab-shack/platform, packages under @crab-shack.
2026-11-10: phase 3 is decomposed. When decomposing this phase, the bead that creates the home dashboard repository uses the product generator and so depends on candy-mountain-v3-8by.4.8 and on the release bead candy-mountain-v3-8by.4.11; the recipes capability comes from the capability generator (8by.4.5).

title: Phase 2: Candy Mountain consumes the release, with a cross-repo development loop
description:
Capability: Candy Mountain installs the platform from the registry at a pinned version, its own platform copies are gone, and a developer can point it at a local base checkout with one command to work on both at once. Plan: .ai-docs/plans/platform-package/phase-2-candy-mountain-consumes.md. Covers replacing the workspace copies of the platform packages with the published ones at the phase-1 version (capability packages and thin apps change only their import sources; the boundary lint keeps enforcing that capabilities import the SDK and nothing deeper, now against installed packages; the copies are deleted so there is one source of truth); one script that links a product to a local base checkout and one that unlinks it, documented in the base's conventions, with the linked state made hard to commit by accident; and the documented upgrade path a product follows when the base releases.

Human test: with Candy Mountain on the registry version, run the pipeline, start the apps and repeat the v3 plan's human tests for issues, chat, bots and uptime. Link to a local base checkout, change a visible string in the platform shell, see it in Candy Mountain without publishing, then unlink and confirm the lock file is unchanged. Publish a patch release of the base, bump Candy Mountain to it and confirm the pipeline is green.
close_reason: Human test passed: confirmed working by kingrea 2026-11-10

title: Phase 1: The base repository: move, name, release, runnable on its own
description:
Capability: the platform lives in its own repository, builds and tests on its own, runs with only the template capability, and publishes versioned packages to the private registry. Plan: .ai-docs/plans/platform-package/phase-1-base-repository.md. Covers creating the base repository and moving the platform packages across with history under the chosen scope while Candy Mountain keeps its copies and stays green; a development distribution (daemon entry and web app assembling the platform with the template capability under a placeholder product name) that the base's tests run against and that proves the platform depends on no Candy Mountain capability; a CI pipeline; package shapes fit for installation without the base's toolchain (built output with type declarations for the daemon-side packages, source for the Nuxt layer); Changesets with one shared version line; a release workflow publishing every platform package at one version to GitHub Packages, private to the organisation; and documentation of how a developer, a CI job and a client repository authenticate to the registry with a read-only token.

Human test: clone the base repository fresh on a machine with no Candy Mountain checkout, authenticate to the registry, install, run the pipeline, start the development distribution and see the template capability's page, table, event and overview card working. Cut a release with a changeset and confirm the packages appear in the organisation's registry at the same version, private, with types.
close_reason: Human test passed: confirmed working by kingrea 2026-11-10

title: Platform package: the platform leaves Candy Mountain for a base repository, a version and a private registry
description:
Capability: the platform packages (platform-daemon, platform-web, platform-sdk, platform-config, platform-cli), the template capability, the test kit and the conventions documents leave the Candy Mountain repository for a base repository of their own, get a name and a version, and are consumed from a private registry (GitHub Packages under the company organisation) by Candy Mountain, a new home dashboard and later the digital hub. The base is proven by a product that is not Candy Mountain, including the single-scope mode the home dashboard needs. At the end, starting a new product or a client-specific capability means a new repo with two short files and a template to copy. Plan: .ai-docs/plans/platform-package/ (overview plus five phase documents). It starts where the platform-extraction plan (epic candy-mountain-v3-ncj) ends and after the product-theme plan (epic candy-mountain-v3-i8n) lands, so the base ships with its theme contract.

Requirements from Jack, not choices to revisit: the base is a separate repository that neither Candy Mountain nor the digital hub is; packages are never public and client-specific capabilities live in client repositories installed only by that client's distribution; capabilities stay unpublished workspace packages inside each product until a third product wants one; the scope entity stays in the model and single-scope products hide it; the base's product name and npm scope are Jack's to choose before phase 1 starts.

Decisions: GitHub Packages as the registry with read-only tokens for consumers (Verdaccio as fallback); Changesets with one shared version line for every platform package, semver meant; a capability declares the SDK major it targets as a peer dependency and the daemon refuses a mismatch at boot naming the package and both versions; git subtree split so history comes along; one documented command each way to link a product to a local base checkout and unlink it, never used in CI; the base contains the platform packages, the template capability, the test kit, the conventions documents and a development distribution that runs the platform with the template alone; uptime and the Slack connection are candidates for standard packages from the base but not in this plan; single-scope mode is product configuration (daemon creates the default workspace at boot, shell hides the picker, auto-selects and redirects, scope label never shown, URL prefix stays); the home dashboard is a new product repo with one capability (recipes) and a native agent; the digital hub becomes a distribution with its capabilities ported one at a time, under its own plan.

Phases: 1 the base repository (move, name, release, runnable on its own); 2 Candy Mountain consumes the release with a cross-repo development loop (after 1); 3 compatibility contract and new-capability scaffold (after 2, alongside 4); 4 home dashboard, the first single-scope product (after 2, alongside 3); 5 digital hub as a distribution, loosely scoped (after 3 and 4, gets its own plan). Per the plan, phases are decomposed one at a time in order; phases 1 and 2 are decomposed together here and phases 3, 4 and 5 are sub-epics awaiting decomposition when phase 2 closes.

Human test: the union of the phase human tests, ending with Candy Mountain, the home dashboard and (in phase 5) the digital hub running on the same base version.

title: Template README: the capability author's guide
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is the first product on a platform that will be extracted to its own repository. A product capability is one package packages/cap-<id> holding a daemon runtime definition under src/ (manifest with views, tools and a rung ladder; routes under the workspace; services with start and close; a schema set with migrations; workspace facts; activity event types) and a Nuxt layer under app/ (gated pages, prefixed components, contributions to the shell such as an overview card). Capability authors are bound by rules enforced by lint: a capability imports a platform package's declared entries only, another capability only through its root entry when dependsOn and package.json both declare it, never a distribution; a layer never imports the platform web package by name, never another layer, and stays under its own prefix and page path. The web conventions document is packages/platform-web/README.md; the daemon conventions document lives in packages/platform-daemon. The template capability packages/cap-template is the complete worked example: one view, one operation tool, one route, one table and migration, one fact, one event type, one service, one gated page, one overview card, and tests on both sides written against the platform's test kit (a daemon test entry point and a web test entry point, each documented where it lives). The template is included in Candy Mountain only in development through a mechanism the distributions' READMEs describe. The planned human test for the whole phase is: copy the template to a new package name, change its id and label, add it to both apps, confirm it appears in the sidebar under a module, its page renders behind the gate, its table exists, its event appears in the activity feed and its card on the overview; run the new package's tests on their own and confirm they pass without the apps; remove it and confirm the pipeline is green.

Problem: the template's README is a title line. The template is only useful if the person copying it knows what each piece is for, what they may and may not change, and what to run; without that it is one more capability to reverse-engineer.

What to write: packages/cap-template/README.md as the capability author's guide, written for an engineer starting a capability (in this repo or, later, in a client repo against the published platform) who has not read the plans. It explains the contract through the template's own pieces: what each file is for and which contribution point it exercises; the rules, each with its reason, pointing at the two conventions documents for depth rather than repeating them; the test kit entries and what the template's tests show; the exact steps to copy the template into a new capability (rename, re-id, regenerate the migration, add to both apps and a module) and to remove one; and the commands to run from the package root and from the repo root. Keep it tight and factual: a reader should be able to execute the human test above from this document alone. Verify every path, command and name against the repo as it is when you write; do not describe what you have not checked.

Non-goals: do not change code. Do not duplicate the conventions documents; link to them.
acceptance_criteria:
- The README covers the template's files and the contribution point each exercises, the rules with reasons and links to both conventions documents, the test kit entries, the copy and remove steps, and the commands.
- Every path, command and name in it exists in the repo; a reviewer following the copy steps from the README alone reaches a package that boots and tests without further guidance.
- pnpm lint passes (the lint checks markdown pointers where it does).
close_reason: Wrote packages/cap-template/README.md (files and contribution points, rules with reasons and links, test kits, copy/add/remove steps verified by a real copy that tested, linted and typechecked alone) and pointers from root, daemon and conventions READMEs

title: The template is included in Candy Mountain only in development, under a module
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is a pnpm workspace. The product is plain data in packages/candy-mountain: the product configuration (name, theme, scope label and URL prefix, and the capability, module, plugin type and layer id lists) and the module definitions (each module a list of members, a capability id with a default rung; a capability appears in the sidebar only through a module the workspace enables). Both distributions read the same object: apps/daemon joins it with the definition factories listed in apps/daemon/src/definitions.ts and refuses to boot when the product data and the definitions disagree; apps/web extends the shell and registers exactly the layers the product lists, and its distribution test keeps that list equal to the layer packages the app depends on. The daemon is started in development with tsx watch and in production from a built bundle; the web app with nuxt dev and nuxt build. Nothing in either distribution today branches on development versus production, and no product field expresses it. A workspace-wide test in apps/daemon refuses a packages/cap-* package the daemon distribution does not list. The template capability packages/cap-template (id template, a page, a route, a table, a fact, an event type, a service and an overview card) now exists and is listed by both distributions like any other capability, but is in no module.

Problem: the template is a worked example for capability authors, not a Candy Mountain feature. It must be seen running in development (sidebar entry under a module, its page behind the gate, its table, its event in the activity feed, its card on the overview) and must be absent from a production build of Candy Mountain, without the product data stopping being plain data and without the two distributions being able to disagree about whether it is there.

What to build: a way for a product to include a capability only in development, applied to the template in Candy Mountain, so that in development both apps include the template and it sits under a module (a development-only module of its own, or membership in an existing one; a module of its own keeps Candy Mountain's real modules clean) and in production neither app knows it. Decide the signal and its shape yourself: the product data stays a plain object both apps and the CLI can read, the daemon's drift check must still fail when the apps would disagree, the distribution tests (the daemon's workspace-wide capability package checks and the web app's layer list check) must express the new invariant rather than being loosened, and a production build must carry no template code. Document the mechanism in both distributions' READMEs where they describe adding a capability, and note it in the product package.

Non-goals: do not add development-only behaviour to the platform packages beyond what a product needs to declare it. Do not change the template itself.
acceptance_criteria:
- In development, the daemon and web app both include the template: it appears in the sidebar under a module once that module is enabled for a workspace, its page renders behind the gate, its table exists, creating a record shows its event in the activity feed and its card on the overview.
- In a production build of both apps the template is absent: not in the registry, not in the sidebar, no layer, no table, and a search of the built output finds no template code.
- The product data remains a plain object; the daemon's drift check and both distributions' tests pass and would fail if one app listed the template and the other did not.
- Both READMEs describe the mechanism; pnpm lint, typecheck, test and build pass from the root.
close_reason: Template included only in development: ProductDevelopment + developmentProductConfig in the SDK, CANDY_MOUNTAIN_DEVELOPMENT/TEMPLATE_MODULE in the product package, daemon src/dev.ts + development.ts and web $development block; builds carry no template code

title: Template capability, web half: gated page, component and overview card, registered with the web app
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is a pnpm workspace. A product capability's UI is a Nuxt layer at the root of its package packages/cap-<id>: pages under app/pages/p/[project]/<id>/ at each manifest view's path, each wrapping its root dashboard panel in the shell's CapabilityViewGate with the capability id and the view id (the gate renders the page only when the actor's rung shows the view and the capability is ready, otherwise a lockout state; the page's own script runs even when locked, so data is fetched by components inside the slot); components under app/components registered with the layer's prefix; prefixed composables and utils; daemon calls through the shell's useApi/$api only; and a Nuxt plugin under app/plugins for contributions to the shell, among them a card on the project overview registered with registerProjectHomeCard(slot, card) (slots are declared in the shell's project-home util; a card takes no props, reads the selected project with useSelectedProject, fetches its own data and renders nothing while it has nothing to show). The web conventions document, packages/platform-web/README.md, states all of this with the import rules: a layer never imports the platform web package by name, never another layer, and never the apps. The product's layers list in packages/candy-mountain/src/product.ts and a dependency line in apps/web/package.json register a layer with the web distribution; apps/web/test/unit/distribution.test.ts keeps the two in step, so both change together. A package packages/cap-template already exists with its configuration (webLayer template, components prefix Template), listed by the daemon distribution; a parallel work item builds its daemon half with a manifest (id template, one view with id template at path template, one operation tool, rungs none, read and manage), a workspace route listing the workspace's records and creating one behind the operation tool, a fact with the record count and an activity event per created record. Agree on the route path with that work by reading the package's src when you start; if it is not there yet, choose the path and leave it in the package README's title line comment for the daemon work to match. A separate work item provides a web test entry point that renders a layer page inside the gate with a registry the test writes; read its documentation in the web conventions document and use only it for page tests.

Problem: the template capability has to show the web half of the contract as plainly as the daemon half: one gated page, one component that talks to the capability's own route, and one card on the overview, built exactly as the conventions ask, so a new capability author copies a correct layer instead of inferring one from issues or bots.

What to build in packages/cap-template/app: the page at the view's path behind the gate, rendering the workspace's records through a prefixed component that fetches them from the template route and offers the create action only to an actor whose registry entry grants the operation tool; a card on the overview in a slot of your choice, showing the record count and rendering nothing when there are no records; and the Nuxt plugin that registers the card. Register the layer with the web distribution: the id in the product's layers list and the dependency line in apps/web, then pnpm install. Tests: through the web test entry point, the page shows its records when the view is granted and the lockout when denied; the overview card renders the count and nothing when empty. Keep every piece the smallest honest version of itself.

Non-goals: do not build the daemon half or the README. Do not add the template to a module or make it development-only (a later work item). Do not restyle anything: rely on the shell's defaults.
acceptance_criteria:
- The template layer has one gated page at the view's path, a prefixed component fetching the template route and creating a record only when the tool is granted, an overview card and the plugin registering it, all passing the layer boundary lint from the package's own root.
- The product's layers list and apps/web list the layer; the web distribution's tests pass.
- The package's web tests import test support only from the web test entry point and pass from the package's own root with the apps absent, covering granted, denied, and the card's empty and non-empty states.
- pnpm lint, typecheck, test and build pass from the root.
close_reason: Template web layer: gated page, TemplateNotes with tool-gated create, useTemplateNotes, aside overview card via plugin, registered in product layers and apps/web, web-kit tests

title: Template capability, daemon half: manifest, route, table, fact, event type and service
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is a pnpm workspace. A product capability is one package packages/cap-<id> whose root entry exports a runtime definition built with the SDK's defineCapabilityDefinition (from @candy-mountain/platform-sdk/daemon): the manifest (built with defineCapability: id, label, description, views with an icon and a path, tools of kind operation, and a ladder of named rungs saying which views and tools each rung grants), an optional dependsOn list, a schema set (a Drizzle schema plus a migrations folder generated by drizzle-kit, applied at boot under a migrations table named for the capability), workspace fact declarations (facts the capability answers for the registry from its own tables), activity event type declarations (ids, labels, icons and the notification kinds they raise), and a start function receiving the platform context (database, data paths, secrets, registries, the scope label and URL prefix, and a service resolver) and returning what the capability runs: workspace routes mounted under the workspace prefix so handlers see the workspace slug, platform routes, service bindings, and a close called in reverse start order. The capability id and the manifest id are the same string. packages/cap-uptime shows a complete small capability; apps/daemon/README.md and the SDK's daemon entry carry the contract. A package packages/cap-template already exists with its configuration files and a placeholder definition with the id template, and the daemon distribution already lists it. A separate work item provides a documented test entry point for the daemon side (a platform from explicit definitions and the app over it, an actor at a chosen rung, a workspace with chosen facts, a plugin instance with fake secrets); read that entry's documentation and use only it for this package's tests.

Problem: the repo has no capability that is small enough to copy and complete enough to show every contribution point at once; a new capability author today reads uptime, issues and bots and guesses which parts are essential. The template capability is that worked example on the daemon side, and the capability author's guide (a later work item) will describe it.

What to build, in packages/cap-template/src, replacing the placeholder: a manifest with id template, label Template, one view (id template, path template) and one operation tool, with a ladder of at least none, read and manage where read sees the view and manage also has the tool; one table holding small per-workspace records (a note, an item: pick something plainly trivial) with one generated migration; a workspace route under the workspace that lists the records and, behind the operation tool, creates one; one workspace fact answered from that table (for instance how many records the workspace holds) declared for the registry; one activity event type appended when a record is created, so the event shows in the workspace's activity feed; a long-running service started in start and stopped in close (something harmless with observable lifecycle, such as a periodic tick that touches nothing outside its own state), so the template demonstrates the lifecycle; and no plugin type, no dependsOn, no chat family. Every piece should be the smallest honest version of itself and carry a terse comment only where the why is not obvious. Tests through the test entry point alone: boot with the template, the route refuses an actor below read and answers one at read, creating a record needs manage and appends the event, the fact reports the count, the service starts and closes cleanly.

Non-goals: do not build the Nuxt layer or the overview card (a parallel work item). Do not write the README (a later work item). Do not add the template to any module or make it development-only (a later work item).
acceptance_criteria:
- The template definition exports the manifest, schema with one migration, one workspace route, one workspace fact, one activity event type and a service with start and close, and the daemon boots with it.
- The package's tests import test support only from the daemon test entry point and pass from the package's own root with the apps absent.
- With a workspace and an actor at manage, creating a record through the route appends the template's event to the workspace activity feed and the fact reports the new count.
- pnpm lint, typecheck, test and build pass from the root.
close_reason: Template daemon half: manifest, template_notes table with 0000_init migration, gated list/create workspace route, hasTemplateNotes fact, template.note.created event, ticker service bound and stopped on close; kit-only tests

title: Scaffold packages/cap-template with its configuration and a placeholder definition listed by the daemon
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is a pnpm workspace. Each product capability is one package packages/cap-<id> holding its daemon runtime definition under src/ and its Nuxt layer under app/, with package.json declaring the layer id in webLayer and exactly one root export. packages/cap-uptime is the closest model for shape: its package.json (scripts typecheck, lint, test, db:generate and db:check; dependencies on the SDK and the daemon platform package; dev dependencies on platform-config and platform-web), tsconfig.json, eslint.config.js (one layerPackageConfig call over the platform-config base), vitest.config.ts (the platform-config preset named for the package), drizzle.config.ts pointing at the package's own migrations folder, and nuxt.config.ts registering components with the capability's prefix. apps/daemon/README.md, under "Adding or removing a capability", lists the exact edits that add a capability package to the Candy Mountain distribution: the dependency line in apps/daemon/package.json, the factory import and entry in apps/daemon/src/definitions.ts, the id in the capabilities list of packages/candy-mountain/src/product.ts, then pnpm install. A workspace-wide test in apps/daemon refuses to pass while a packages/cap-* package exists that the daemon distribution does not list, so a new package must enter the distribution in the same change.

Problem: phase 5 adds a template capability, packages/cap-template with capability id template, a deliberately small capability that exercises every contribution point and is the thing to copy when starting a new capability. Its daemon half and its web half are built by separate work items that run in parallel, so the package itself, with its configuration and its place in the daemon distribution, has to exist first.

What to do: create packages/cap-template (package name @candy-mountain/cap-template, webLayer template, components prefix Template) with every configuration file the uptime package has, adjusted to the new name and prefix, an empty migrations folder for drizzle, a README holding only a title line, and a root entry exporting a placeholder definition with the id template and nothing else (no manifest, no start), so the package is a valid capability package. Add it to the daemon distribution following the README's steps: dependency line, definitions entry placed last before platform-agent, the id in the product's capabilities list, pnpm install. Do not add it to apps/web, the product's layers list or any module: the layer does not exist yet and those are later work items. Do not write the real definition, schema, routes, pages or README content.
acceptance_criteria:
- packages/cap-template exists with the configuration files listed, builds its placeholder definition from the SDK's define helper, and is listed by the daemon distribution and the product's capabilities list.
- pnpm install, then pnpm lint, typecheck, test and build from the root pass, including the daemon distribution's workspace-wide capability package tests.
- Starting the daemon still works and the template appears in no module, sidebar or registry.
- apps/web, the product's layers list and the module definitions are unchanged.
close_reason: cap-template scaffolded with placeholder definition, listed in daemon distribution and product capabilities

title: Move every capability package's daemon tests onto the test kit
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is a pnpm workspace run through Turborepo. Each product capability is a package packages/cap-<id>, each plugin type a connection package packages/plugin-<id>; both hold a daemon runtime definition under src/ with tests beside it. Until now their tests imported test support (an in-memory database over chosen definitions, a platform started from explicit definitions, an app over it, fixture manifests and definitions, a plugin-instance harness, grant fixtures, a stub gateway) from the daemon platform package's production root entry, and some assembled an actor, a workspace, a grant or a plugin instance by hand from several platform calls. A separate work item has introduced one documented test entry point for the daemon side that offers all of that (a platform from explicit definitions and the app over it, an actor at a chosen rung, a workspace with chosen facts, a plugin instance with fake secrets, plus the earlier fixtures) and has stopped exporting test support from the daemon platform's production root. Read that entry's documentation first; it names where the entry lives and what each helper gives.

Problem: the capability packages' tests still reach the old places. They must become the first real consumers of the test kit so that the kit is proven on every capability's shape (routes, services, schema, facts, event types, plugin types with secrets) and so that no capability test depends on anything the follow-on plan will not publish with the platform.

What to do: move every test in every cap-* and plugin-* package onto the test entry point. Where a test builds an actor, workspace, grant or plugin instance by hand, use the kit's helper instead when it covers the case; where the kit lacks something several tests need, add it to the kit rather than keeping a local workaround, and document the addition. Tests must keep their intent and assertions; this is a change of fixtures, not of what is tested. The distribution's own product-aware helpers in apps/daemon/src/testing stay for the distribution's tests, but no capability package may import them.

Non-goals: do not change capability behaviour. Do not touch the web layers or their tests.
acceptance_criteria:
- No file under packages/cap-*/src or packages/plugin-*/src imports test support from anywhere but the test entry point; a repo-wide search proves it.
- No capability package imports apps/daemon or its testing helpers.
- Every capability package's test suite passes from its own root.
- pnpm lint, typecheck, test and build pass from the root.
close_reason: Every cap-*/plugin-* test (except cap-template) runs on @candy-mountain/platform-daemon/testing with kit actors/workspaces/plugin instances; kit gained restart, as and deps; gates green except known 5qz

title: Daemon conventions document in the daemon platform package
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is a pnpm workspace whose platform is being extracted so other products can consume it. packages/platform-daemon is the daemon platform (database and migration sets applied in dependency order each under its own migrations table, auth, workspaces, registries, grants, plugin instances and secrets, activity, notifications, the app factory and the platform start function; one root entry) and packages/platform-sdk carries the contract a capability writes against: a runtime definition (id equal to the manifest id; an optional manifest; dependsOn; plugin types for connection packages; session families; provided service keys; a schema set with a migrations folder; activity event type and workspace fact declarations; a start function receiving the platform context and returning services, workspace and platform routes, MCP servers, chat families, notification channels, workspace agents, a workspace-deletion hook and a close). The SDK's daemon entry documents each field in comments. The daemon applies definitions in registration order, binds the services a definition provides for its dependents, starts the platform's own definitions first, closes in reverse order, and validates ids, dependencies, required plugin types and facts at boot so a bad definition stops the daemon with a message naming it. The package-boundary lint in packages/platform-config (its DIRECTIONS text and its rule messages) enforces that a capability imports a platform package's declared entries only, another capability only through its root entry when dependsOn and package.json both declare it, never a distribution, and that only a plugin-<id> connection package brings plugin types; its rule docs point at a README that explains the rules. Today the explanation of all this is spread across apps/daemon/README.md (which describes the distribution and also much of the platform's shape, how to add a capability, variables, and subsystems), the SDK's comments and the lint's messages. The web side already has its conventions document, packages/platform-web/README.md, with sections on registration, directory shape, routes, the gate, dependency directions, boundary lint and contribution points, and the web lint's rule docs point at it.

Problem: a capability author on the daemon side has no single document stating what a runtime definition is, how its services live and die, who owns which tables, and what it may import and depend on. When the platform leaves this repository the daemon distribution's README leaves with Candy Mountain, so the platform's own rules must live in the platform package where any product's capability author finds them.

What to write: the daemon conventions document in packages/platform-daemon (its README), the counterpart of the web conventions document, written for a capability author rather than a platform maintainer. It covers: the runtime definition and each of its parts, in prose with the reasons (why ids are open validated strings registered at boot, why the manifest is separate from the runtime, why a connection package has no manifest); the service lifecycle (start order, dependency binding and the service resolver, platform routes versus workspace routes and what the workspace prefix gives a handler, close order, the workspace deletion hook and its after-commit rule); schema ownership (one schema set per package, the migrations folder generated with drizzle-kit, the per-capability migrations table, which platform tables a capability may reference and how, what a capability must never touch); the dependency declaration (dependsOn and package.json must agree, what crossing a root entry means, what is refused at boot and what is refused at lint, with the lint rule names); and what the platform promises to keep stable for a capability versus what is internal. Point the package-boundary lint's rule docs at this document instead of the root README, and reduce apps/daemon/README.md to the distribution's own concerns (its shape, adding a capability to Candy Mountain, its variables and subsystems) with a link to the conventions for the contract, removing text the new document now owns. Verify every name against the code; do not describe behaviour you have not read.

Non-goals: do not change code other than the lint's documentation pointer. Do not write the capability author's guide or document the test kit (other work items). Do not duplicate the web conventions document.
acceptance_criteria:
- packages/platform-daemon has a conventions document with the five areas above, each with reasons, and every name in it exists in the code.
- The package-boundary lint's rule docs name that document; the lint's own test still passes.
- apps/daemon/README.md no longer explains the capability contract itself and links to the conventions document; nothing it still says contradicts it.
- pnpm lint and test pass from the root.
close_reason: Daemon conventions doc written in packages/platform-daemon/README.md; cm-packages rule docs point at it; apps/daemon README trimmed to distribution concerns with links. Root lint green; root test red only from 5.1's in-flight removal of root test exports.

title: Web test kit: render a layer page inside the gate with a registry the test writes
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is a pnpm workspace run through Turborepo. packages/platform-web is the web shell, a Nuxt layer that a distribution extends; its README is the web conventions document. A product capability's UI is a Nuxt layer at the root of its package packages/cap-<id> (package.json declares webLayer, nuxt.config registers prefixed components), with pages under app/pages/p/[project]/<id>/ that wrap their root in the shell's CapabilityViewGate component with the capability id and the manifest view id. The gate reads the project's registry (the shell's useProjectRegistry composable, fed by the daemon) and renders the page's slot only when the actor's rung shows the view and the capability is ready for the project; otherwise it renders a lockout state (plugins to configure, module not enabled, or not available to you). Pages and components reach the shell only through Nuxt auto-imports (components, composables, utils) and the shell's useApi/$api for daemon calls. Each layer package runs vitest from its own root through the platform-config preset, with no Nuxt environment: today every web test in the repo is a plain unit test of utils and registries, and no package installs component mounting tooling (no @vue/test-utils, no @nuxt/test-utils). The lint rule cm-layers/no-platform-package-import forbids a layer importing @candy-mountain/platform-web by name, exempting only the layer's root eslint and vitest configs; the boundary lint's fixtures (a layered app with delta and epsilon layer packages and a stand-in platform layer under packages/platform-web/test/fixtures) exercise the rules.

Problem: a capability cannot test its page as users meet it. There is no way to render a layer page behind the gate with a registry that grants or denies the view, so whether a page locks out correctly and shows its content when allowed is only ever checked by hand in the running app. A capability in another repository, built against published platform packages, has the same gap. The platform-extraction plan asks for the web half of a test kit: a way to mount a layer page inside the gate with a registry that grants or denies the view, importable from the capability's own package with the apps absent.

What to build: a web test entry point that a capability's web test imports and nothing else, giving it a way to render one of its own pages (or components) inside the shell's gate with a selected project, a registry the test writes (the capability at a chosen rung with the view granted, or denied, or the capability not ready) and daemon calls the test answers, and to assert on what rendered. Decide the mounting approach and its tooling yourself; whatever you choose must run from a layer package's own root under the existing vitest preset, must cope with a page that uses auto-imported shell names (the gate component, the registry and project composables) and must not require the Candy Mountain apps. Decide where the entry lives: the lint exempts only root config files from importing the platform web package by name, so either extend that exemption to test files or the test entry, or house the entry where a layer may already import from; keep the rule honest for layer source files either way and extend the lint's fixture test for whichever you choose. Document the entry in the web conventions document: how a layer test renders a page, what the registry fake accepts, what the kit never does.

Non-goals: do not change the gate's behaviour or the registry's shape. Do not migrate existing layer tests. Do not build the daemon side; that is a separate work item.
acceptance_criteria:
- A test in the platform web package renders a fixture layer's page through the entry with the view granted and sees the page's content, with the view denied and sees the lockout state and no page content, and with the capability not ready and sees the configure state.
- The same kind of test runs from a layer package's own root under the existing vitest preset without a Nuxt dev server and without importing the apps.
- Lint still refuses a layer source file that imports the platform web package by name, and the boundary lint's fixture test covers the exemption or placement chosen for the test entry.
- The web conventions document describes the entry.
- pnpm lint, typecheck, test and build pass from the root.

title: Daemon test kit: one test entry point a capability's tests import, nothing from the apps
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is a pnpm workspace run through Turborepo (pnpm lint, typecheck, test and build from the root; each package also runs them from its own root through the presets in packages/platform-config). The platform is packages/platform-daemon (database and migration sets, auth, workspaces, registries, grants, plugin instances and secrets, activity, the app factory and the platform start function; one root entry), packages/platform-sdk (shared types and the define helpers; a root entry and a ./daemon entry; the package a capability's contract comes from) and packages/platform-config (presets and the package-boundary lint). A product capability is one package packages/cap-<id> (or a connection package packages/plugin-<id>) holding a runtime definition under src/: manifest, routes, services with start and close, a schema set with a migrations folder, workspace facts, activity event types, plugin types. The product package packages/candy-mountain is plain data; apps/daemon is the thin distribution that lists definition factories and starts the platform. Lint rules: a capability imports a platform package's declared entries only, never its internals, another capability only through its root entry when dependsOn and package.json both declare it, and never a distribution.

Problem: a capability's daemon tests today lean on test support that is not theirs. The daemon platform package's production root entry exports its test helpers (an in-memory database over chosen definitions, a platform started from explicit definitions, an app over it, fixture manifests and definitions, a plugin-instance harness, grant and access fixtures, a stub gateway), so every capability test imports them from the same entry that production code imports, and nothing marks which exports are test support. The distribution adds product-aware wrappers in apps/daemon/src/testing that default everything to Candy Mountain and to workspaces carrying a repository, and some capability tests still assemble an actor, a workspace, a grant and a plugin instance by hand from several platform calls. A capability written in another repository, against published platform packages, would have none of this. The follow-on plan moves the platform packages out of this repo, so what a capability needs to test itself has to travel with the platform as one documented test entry point.

What to build: one test entry point for the daemon side that a capability's tests import and nothing else. The platform-extraction plan names it the SDK's test entry point. The SDK today has no runtime dependency on the daemon platform package while the daemon platform package depends on the SDK, and starting a platform needs the daemon platform's start function; resolve that direction yourself (a test subpath on the SDK that reaches the daemon platform package, a test subpath on the daemon platform package, or another arrangement) without creating a typecheck or lint cycle, and record the choice and its reason in the entry's documentation. Through that entry a test can: start a platform in a temporary data directory with only the platform's own definitions plus the definitions the test names (the capability under test and any it depends on), and get the app over it for route tests; obtain an actor at a chosen rung of a chosen capability in a chosen workspace, with a session or header the app accepts; create a workspace with chosen facts; create a plugin instance of a chosen type with fake secrets, without a real secrets key; and close everything down. Keep the existing lower-level helpers reachable through the same entry where a test still needs them (fixture manifests and definitions, the in-memory database, the instance harness), and move or re-export rather than rewrite what already works. The entry is documented beside the package that owns it (a README section or the package's conventions document): what each helper gives, what it never does, and that it is the only thing a capability's tests import from the platform.

Hard requirements: a capability's tests never import apps/daemon or apps/web, and the boundary lint says so when one does (if the lint already refuses a capability importing a distribution package, add the case to the lint's fixture test so it stays refused; otherwise add the rule). The daemon platform package's production root entry stops exporting test support once the entry exists; the daemon's own tests and the distribution's tests may keep using internal helpers through relative paths as they do now. Do not migrate the existing capability packages' tests in this work item; that is a separate item that runs after this one. Do not touch the web side.
acceptance_criteria:
- One documented test entry point exists for the daemon side; its documentation states where it lives, why, what each helper does and that a capability's tests import nothing else from the platform.
- A test in the platform's own suite uses the entry to start a platform with one fixture definition, an actor at a chosen rung, a workspace with a chosen fact and a plugin instance with fake secrets, and proves the route gate admits that actor and refuses one at a lower rung.
- The daemon platform package's production root entry no longer exports test support; the platform's own tests and the distribution's tests still pass.
- Lint reports a capability test file that imports a distribution package by name, and the boundary lint's fixture test proves it.
- pnpm lint, typecheck, test and build pass from the root.
close_reason: Daemon test kit at @candy-mountain/platform-daemon/testing (testKit: platform+app, actor at a rung, workspace with facts, plugin instance with fake secrets, close), documented in packages/platform-daemon/TESTING.md; root entry exports no test support; cm-packages/no-distribution-import added with fixture test; root lint, typecheck, test (bar known 5qz failure) and build green.

title: cap-issues as the worked example: prefixed variables derived from the shell that a product can override
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is a pnpm workspace. The web shell is @candy-mountain/platform-web (packages/platform-web), a Nuxt layer a distribution (apps/web) extends; every capability's UI is a Nuxt layer at the root of its capability package (packages/cap-<id>, packages/plugin-<id>, package.json "webLayer": "<id>"), and the shell holds two layers of its own under layers/ (chat, shared infrastructure, and overview). Core is the shell's own app/, server/ and shared/. The shell owns the neutral palette in app/assets/css/main.css (the --ui-bg*, --ui-text*, --ui-border*, --ui-radius, --ui-header-height, --app-bg-canvas and --app-bg-shell variables for :root and .dark, plus a Tailwind @theme block) and the Nuxt UI component defaults in app/app.config.ts under the ui key; layers inherit both, and a layer's own app/app.config.ts deep-merges into the app config, which is how a layer contributes to the shell's registration keys (chat and project-home contributions) today. Import boundaries are enforced by a local ESLint plugin, cm-layers, in packages/platform-web/eslint/layer-boundaries.mjs (exported as @candy-mountain/platform-web/eslint): its rules (no-cross-layer-import, no-cross-layer-auto-import, no-platform-package-import, layer-prefix, layer-pages) know which layer owns each file from where it lives, run for every script and .vue file under the linted root from apps/web and from the package's own eslint.config.mjs, and run for each layer package from its own root through layerPackageConfig, reporting what linting it from the app would. Every message points at packages/platform-web/README.md, the web conventions document, whose Boundary lint section lists the rules. packages/platform-web/test/unit/layer-boundaries.test.ts lints the fixture app in test/fixtures/layered-app (directory layers alpha, beta, gadget), the linked layer packages test/fixtures/delta-layer and test/fixtures/epsilon-layer, and test/fixtures/platform-layer standing in for the shell, and asserts each rule fires for directory layers, package layers and the shell's own layers alike, and that linting a layer package from its own root reports the same findings as linting the app; the fixtures are ignored by the normal lint. Existing capability styling is small: cap-issues has scoped style blocks (one reads shell variables such as --ui-border-accented, one uses :deep()), and connection packages ship SVG icon assets. Gates: pnpm lint, pnpm --recursive --workspace-concurrency=1 typecheck (parallel typechecks are killed for memory on this machine), pnpm test and pnpm build green. Do not commit.

This bead is part of the product-theme work (plan: .ai-docs/plans/product-theme/overview.md): a product defines its whole look in its product configuration and a product stylesheet that the shell loads after its own, and a capability styles only what it brings. The capability rules: a layer may use per-instance ui overrides on Nuxt UI components, components it wraps under its own prefix, scoped style blocks, and its own custom properties named with its layer prefix, set on its own root elements and derived from the shell's variables so a product theme flows through them. A layer may never register a stylesheet through its layer config, write an unscoped or :global style block, select the document root, html, body or the colour-mode class, assign any shell (--ui-*, --app-*) or Tailwind theme variable, declare Tailwind theme, base-layer or utility blocks, or set the Nuxt UI key (ui) in its app config. CSS has no sandbox, so the boundary is what a layer is allowed to write, and the platform enforces it rather than trusting the author. A product restyles a capability only by setting the capability's prefixed variables from the product stylesheet.

Problem: the capability styling convention says a layer's own custom properties are named with its prefix, set on its own root elements and derived from the shell's variables, so that a product theme flows through them and a product can override exactly that capability from its stylesheet. No capability does this yet, so the convention has no worked example and nothing proves that a product can reach one capability and nothing else. cap-issues (packages/cap-issues, layer id issues) is the one capability with real scoped CSS: its dependency graph component reads shell variables such as --ui-border-accented directly in a scoped style block, and its markdown component uses :deep() in one.

What to build: bring cap-issues in line as the worked example. Its scoped styles read the layer's own prefixed custom properties instead of shell variables directly; those properties are declared on the layer's own root elements (the elements its components render, never the document) with values derived from the shell's variables, so the default look is unchanged in both colour modes and a product theme that changes the shell's variables still reaches the graph. At least one of them is a knob a product would plausibly turn (the graph edge colour is the obvious one). The layer keeps to the allowed forms only: scoped blocks, prefixed properties, no global selectors, no shell variable assignment, no stylesheet in its config, no ui key in its app config. Note in the cap-issues package what the properties are and that a product sets them from its stylesheet, in the terse comment style the repository uses.

Non-goals: no visual change by default; no change to the shell or to any other capability; no product stylesheet override shipped in Candy Mountain, whose look must not change (the override is exercised by hand in the epic's human test).

Acceptance: the issues pages look the same as before in light and dark mode; a scratch override of the edge-colour property in a stylesheet loaded after the shell's changes the graph's edges and nothing else; cap-issues lints clean from its own root and from apps/web. Root gates green.
notes: Published knob --issues-graph-edge (read only, fallback --ui-border-accented) via working prop --issues-graph-edge-color on .issues-graph; markdown uses working props on .issues-markdown, no knobs. Verified in headless Chromium with Vue-compiled scoped CSS: 0 computed-style diffs vs HEAD in light/dark; :root/.dark override after the shell changes only edge stroke and arrow fill. Scoped lint/test/typecheck green; root lint+typecheck green; root test (platform-web layer-list fixture 'styled') and build (platform-web/modules/platform-web.ts:44) fail on other agents' in-flight work.
close_reason: Closed

title: Conventions document: the shell's variables as the theme contract and the product theme fields
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is a pnpm workspace of platform packages (packages/platform-sdk, platform-web, platform-daemon, platform-config, platform-cli), capability packages (packages/cap-* and packages/plugin-*, each a daemon definition under src/ and a Nuxt web layer at the package root), a plain-data product package (packages/candy-mountain exports CANDY_MOUNTAIN_PRODUCT, a ProductConfig from @candy-mountain/platform-sdk: name, description, theme, scope and the capability, module, plugin type and layer id lists) and thin apps (apps/daemon, apps/web). The web shell is @candy-mountain/platform-web, a Nuxt layer that a distribution extends: apps/web/nuxt.config.ts extends it and hands over the product through the platformWeb: { product } option of the package's Nuxt module (packages/platform-web/modules/platform-web.ts), which writes the configuration into a virtual module the shell reads as PRODUCT (shared/utils/product.ts) and pushes the theme hex into the theme-color meta; server/utils/web-manifest.ts builds the PWA manifest from it. The daemon reads the same ProductConfig, so it must stay plain JSON data with no file paths or functions. The shell's playground (packages/platform-web/playground, product in playground/product.ts as PLAYGROUND_PRODUCT) runs the shell with no capability layer and is what the package's lint, typecheck and unit tests run against. Today ProductTheme is just a Nuxt UI colour name (primary) and a hex. app/app.config.ts sets ui.colors.primary from it and neutral to 'neutral' and holds the shell's component defaults; app/assets/css/main.css, the only shell stylesheet (loaded through the shell nuxt.config css option), sets the --ui-bg*, --ui-text*, --ui-border*, --ui-radius, --ui-header-height, --app-bg-canvas and --app-bg-shell variables for :root and for .dark; app/components/AppHeader.vue and app/pages/login.vue hardcode the i-lucide-mountain-snow icon beside the product name; app/layouts/dashboard.vue always renders UColorModeButton. Nuxt UI v4 brings the fonts module, so a font family named in the sans or mono font variables is fetched without any new module, and Nuxt UI resolves colour aliases against Tailwind's colour theme, so a colour outside Tailwind's palette needs its scale declared in CSS. packages/platform-web/README.md is the web conventions document. Plugin icons already use one shape for "an icon or an image": either an icon name as UIcon takes it, or an image URL plus classes for the img element, rendered by core's PluginsIcon component. Gates: pnpm lint, pnpm --recursive --workspace-concurrency=1 typecheck (parallel typechecks are killed for memory on this machine), pnpm test and pnpm build green. Do not commit.

This bead is part of the product-theme work (plan: .ai-docs/plans/product-theme/overview.md), which lands before the platform packages leave this repository so the base ships with a theme contract: a product defines its whole look in its product configuration and a distribution-owned stylesheet, and a capability styles only what it brings.

Problem: a theme that augments the shell needs to know what the shell exposes, and today the shell's surface, text, border, radius and app-chrome variables are treated as private: the conventions document's Shared visual system section describes the palette's intent and utilities but not the variables as something a product may set, and nothing documents the product theme fields, the stylesheet handover or how a product changes component defaults. Documenting the existing set costs nothing and makes a product theme reviewable.

What to build: in packages/platform-web/README.md, add a product theme section (and adjust the Shared visual system section so the two agree) that states the contract: every field of the product configuration's theme section and what the shell does with each (aliases into Nuxt UI's colour config, hex into the manifest and meta, logo into the header and login page, colour mode into the module default and the toggle's visibility; read the real field names from ProductTheme in @candy-mountain/platform-sdk and the real handover from the shell's Nuxt module in packages/platform-web/modules/platform-web.ts); the full list of shell variables a product may set, in both colour modes, as the token list, taken from app/assets/css/main.css; that a custom colour alias needs its scale declared in the product stylesheet and that an undeclared one fails the build; that the typeface is set through the sans and mono font variables with no new field or module; that component defaults stay in the shell's app config and a product changes them from the distribution's own app config, which Nuxt lets win over every layer (documented, not built); and that a product restyles a capability only by setting that capability's prefixed variables from the product stylesheet. Include one example product stylesheet that declares a custom colour scale, a typeface and a dark-mode override of a shell variable; the playground product in packages/platform-web/playground is being given a full theme in parallel, so name it as the running example without depending on its exact values. A capability-styling section is being written to the same document by another bead; add your section beside it and do not rewrite other sections.

Non-goals: no code change; no change to the plan documents.

Acceptance: a product author reading only the README can write a product theme and stylesheet for a new distribution without opening shell source; every variable in main.css appears in the token list; the field names match the SDK type; lint passes on the document if the repo lints markdown. Root gates green.

The capability rules: a layer may use per-instance ui overrides on Nuxt UI components, components it wraps under its own prefix, scoped style blocks, and its own custom properties named with its layer prefix, set on its own root elements and derived from the shell's variables so a product theme flows through them. A layer may never register a stylesheet through its layer config, write an unscoped or :global style block, select the document root, html, body or the colour-mode class, assign any shell (--ui-*, --app-*) or Tailwind theme variable, declare Tailwind theme, base-layer or utility blocks, or set the Nuxt UI key (ui) in its app config. CSS has no sandbox, so the boundary is what a layer is allowed to write, and the platform enforces it rather than trusting the author. A product restyles a capability only by setting the capability's prefixed variables from the product stylesheet.

Problem: a capability layer inherits the shell's look by convention only. Nothing stops a layer shipping an unscoped style block or an imported stylesheet that resets the shell's variables or restyles another capability, and the first product that is not Candy Mountain will find out the hard way. CSS has no sandbox, so the boundary is what a layer is allowed to write, and the lint that already knows which layer owns each file is the place to enforce it.

What to build: a new cm-layers rule in packages/platform-web/eslint/layer-boundaries.mjs that applies to every file owned by a layer other than core (every layer package and the shell's own chat and overview layers alike; core's own app is exempt) and refuses, in a .vue file's style blocks and in any stylesheet file the layer imports from a script or component (an imported sheet is global by nature, so it is refused outright, as is a style block loaded from a src attribute): a style block that is not scoped (a CSS-modules block counts as scoped); any :global or v-global selector; any selector that reaches the document root, html, body or the colour-mode class; any declaration that assigns a shell variable (the --ui-* and --app-* families) or a Tailwind theme variable, which for this rule means any custom property that does not carry the layer's own prefix; any Tailwind theme, base-layer or utility declaration. The rule runs from the app and from a layer package's own root through layerPackageConfig with the same findings. title: Playground product uses every theme field with a colour outside Tailwind's palette
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is a pnpm workspace of platform packages (packages/platform-sdk, platform-web, platform-daemon, platform-config, platform-cli), capability packages (packages/cap-* and packages/plugin-*, each a daemon definition under src/ and a Nuxt web layer at the package root), a plain-data product package (packages/candy-mountain exports CANDY_MOUNTAIN_PRODUCT, a ProductConfig from @candy-mountain/platform-sdk: name, description, theme, scope and the capability, module, plugin type and layer id lists) and thin apps (apps/daemon, apps/web). The sheet is a file path handed to the module, not a field of the product configuration, because that configuration is serialised into a virtual module and read by the daemon. When a colour alias in the product theme names a colour that is neither a Tailwind palette nor a scale the product stylesheet declares, the build must fail with a message naming the alias and the undeclared colour; find out whether Nuxt UI or Tailwind already fail this way, and if they do not, the shell's module performs the check itself from the aliases and the sheet it was given. description:

title: Conventions documents and plans describe connection packages
description:
Context: Candy Mountain v3 is a pnpm workspace made of platform packages (packages/platform-daemon, platform-web, platform-sdk, platform-config, platform-cli), capability packages (packages/cap-<id>: a daemon definition under src/ behind the root entry, and a Nuxt web layer at the package root with package.json "webLayer": "<layer id>"), a plain-data product package (packages/candy-mountain: CANDY_MOUNTAIN_PRODUCT lists the capability, module, plugin type and layer ids; MODULES groups capabilities), and two thin apps (apps/daemon registers every definition in src/definitions.ts and builds the Product in src/candy-mountain.ts; apps/web depends on every layer package and lists nothing else). A capability definition is made with defineCapabilityDefinition from @candy-mountain/platform-sdk/daemon: id, optional manifest (absent means service-only: in no catalog, module or grant), dependsOn, pluginTypes, sessionFamilies, provides (service keys), schema, activityEventTypes, workspaceFacts, and start(context) returning services, workspace and platform routes, MCP servers, notification channels, chat families and close; context.service(key) resolves only keys bound by a declared dependency, and start order follows dependsOn. A plugin type is defined with definePluginType from @candy-mountain/platform-daemon (id, config fields, secret fields, health check, admin actions, delete hook); plugin instances are per workspace and platform-owned; a manifest's requiresPlugins and requiresAnyPlugins name plugin type ids and the gate checks the workspace has instances; the daemon refuses duplicate plugin type ids and refuses a required type that no definition or product supplies. Import rules are enforced by the ESLint plugin cm-packages (packages/platform-config/eslint/package-boundaries.mjs, which keys package kinds on the @candy-mountain/platform- and @candy-mountain/cap- name prefixes and checks that a capability package's package.json dependencies on capability packages and its definition's dependsOn agree) and cm-layers (packages/platform-web/eslint/layer-boundaries.mjs): a capability imports platform-sdk and the root entry of platform-daemon; another capability only via its root entry and only when dependsOn and package.json both name it; the platform never imports a capability; a web layer imports core and the chat layer only, so cross-capability UI goes through core contribution points (registerPluginIcon, registerPluginPanel, registerPluginForm, chatFamilyRegister, registerProjectHomeCard and friends), and every name a layer auto-registers carries the layer's prefix. The daemon's assertProduct refuses to boot when the product's id lists and the supplied definitions disagree in either direction, so every supplied capability id, service-only ones included, is listed in CANDY_MOUNTAIN_PRODUCT.capabilities; apps/web/test/unit/distribution.test.ts forces CANDY_MOUNTAIN_PRODUCT.layers to equal the layer packages the web app depends on plus the shell's own layers. packages/platform-web/README.md is the web conventions document.

The change this epic makes (plan: .ai-docs/plans/connection-packages/overview.md): today three feature capabilities bring plugin types (chat-claude-code brings claude-code, chat-codex brings codex, deployments brings netlify and heroku) and the ACP session runtime (harness, session manager, decisions, their routes, the ACP_SESSIONS/ACP_HARNESS/ACP_DECISIONS keys) lives inside cap-chat-claude-code, so chat-codex and bots depend on a chat UI capability to run agents, and a second published capability needing the same connection would have to define the type again and collide at boot. The new convention: a connection package named @candy-mountain/plugin-<id> is a service-only capability definition (no manifest) whose id equals the id of the plugin type it brings, and is the only kind of package allowed to bring plugin types; it may provide services, declare schema, mount routes and declare facts, and has a web layer when its plugin type needs UI. A feature capability (@candy-mountain/cap-<id>, has a manifest) requires plugin types and depends on connection packages for their services. A service-only package that brings no plugin type keeps the cap- prefix. Target layout: plugin-repository and plugin-slack (renames of cap-repository and cap-slack), plugin-claude-code, plugin-codex, plugin-heroku and plugin-netlify (new), cap-acp (new, service-only, id acp: the ACP runtime, depending on threads and repository), with cap-chat-claude-code, cap-chat-codex, cap-deployments and cap-bots depending on them. Capability ids, plugin type ids, layer ids, table names, routes and stored data do not change unless a bead says so. Working pieces move as they are: no redesign and no behaviour change beyond what this bead asks. Gates: pnpm lint, pnpm --recursive --workspace-concurrency=1 typecheck (parallel typechecks are killed for memory on this machine), pnpm test and pnpm build green. Do not commit.


Problem: the conventions documents still describe plugin types as living in the capability that brings them, the package list in the platform-extraction plan says there is no plugin-type-only package, and the platform-package plan's generators are described as producing one kind of capability package. A capability author reading them after this epic would build the old shape.

What to build: bring the written conventions in line with the connection-package convention. The web conventions document (packages/platform-web/README.md) describes plugin- packages as layer packages with their own layer id and says a plugin type's UI lives in the connection package's layer. Whatever daemon-side conventions text exists (the package boundary lint's DOCS pointer names it) states the rule: a plugin- package is a service-only definition whose id is its plugin type's id, the only kind allowed to bring plugin types; a cap- package never does; a service-only package bringing no plugin type keeps the cap- prefix. The platform-package plan's phase 3 document gains one paragraph saying the capability generator offers both shapes and that the compatibility check applies to connection packages the same way. The platform-extraction overview's decision that said there is no plugin-type-only package gets a one-line note pointing to the connection-packages plan as the later decision, without rewriting history. Mentions of cap-repository or cap-slack as reference packages are updated to the new names.

Non-goals: no code changes; no rewriting of landed plan documents beyond the pointer.

Acceptance: searching the conventions documents and the two plans for the old statement (a plugin type lives in the capability that brings it, or no plugin-type-only package) finds only the historical note with its pointer. The web README's example package paths resolve to packages that exist.
close_reason: Conventions docs and plans describe plugin-/cap- connection packages; ACP and plugin-type paths updated

Problem: cap-deployments brings the netlify and heroku plugin types together with the API clients and operations that talk to those services, and also owns the live-version sources that read a deployed version through them. Problem: with every plugin type now brought by a plugin- package, nothing yet stops the next capability author from putting a plugin type back into a feature capability, or from publishing a plugin- package that also carries a manifest. A capability definition is made with defineCapabilityDefinition from @candy-mountain/platform-sdk/daemon: id, optional manifest (absent means service-only: in no catalog, module or grant), dependsOn, pluginTypes, sessionFamilies, provides (service keys), schema, activityEventTypes, workspaceFacts, and start(context) returning services, workspace and platform routes, MCP servers, notification channels, chat families and close; context.service(key) resolves only keys bound by a declared dependency, and start order follows dependsOn. A plugin type is defined with definePluginType from @candy-mountain/platform-daemon (id, config fields, secret fields, health check, admin actions, delete hook); plugin instances are per workspace and platform-owned; a manifest's requiresPlugins and requiresAnyPlugins name plugin type ids and the gate checks the workspace has instances; the daemon refuses duplicate plugin type ids and refuses a required type that no definition or product supplies. Import rules are enforced by the ESLint plugin cm-packages (packages/platform-config/eslint/package-boundaries.mjs, which keys package kinds on the @candy-mountain/platform- and @candy-mountain/cap- name prefixes and checks that a capability package's package.json dependencies on capability packages and its definition's dependsOn agree) and cm-layers (packages/platform-web/eslint/layer-boundaries.mjs): a capability imports platform-sdk and the root entry of platform-daemon; another capability only via its root entry and only when dependsOn and package.json both name it; the platform never imports a capability; a web layer imports core and the chat layer only, so cross-capability UI goes through core contribution points (registerPluginIcon, registerPluginPanel, registerPluginForm, chatFamilyRegister, registerProjectHomeCard and friends), and every name a layer auto-registers carries the layer's prefix. The daemon's assertProduct refuses to boot when the product's id lists and the supplied definitions disagree in either direction, so every supplied capability id, service-only ones included, is listed in CANDY_MOUNTAIN_PRODUCT.capabilities; apps/web/test/unit/distribution.test.ts forces CANDY_MOUNTAIN_PRODUCT.layers to equal the layer packages the web app depends on plus the shell's own layers. packages/platform-web/README.md is the web conventions document.

The change this epic makes (plan: .ai-docs/plans/connection-packages/overview.md): today three feature capabilities bring plugin types (chat-claude-code brings claude-code, chat-codex brings codex, deployments brings netlify and heroku) and the ACP session runtime (harness, session manager, decisions, their routes, the ACP_SESSIONS/ACP_HARNESS/ACP_DECISIONS keys) lives inside cap-chat-claude-code, so chat-codex and bots depend on a chat UI capability to run agents, and a second published capability needing the same connection would have to define the type again and collide at boot.
